Dear County Councilors,

Affordable housing is an emergency and needs to be treated like the
crisis it is. During your public hearing on October 1, please add a
commitment to set affordable housing goals, track progress, and
adjust as needed, using the data already being provided to the
county by the state under SB 5587, which passed in 2025.

Setting goals, tracking progress, and adjusting as needed is
fundamental for responsible management toward any goal, and
affordable housing certainly deserves this level of seriousness and
focus. Failing to set goals and track whether you are meeting them
indicates a lack of seriousness regarding the affordable housing
crisis that impacts so many Clark County families.

On October 1, please establish in the comprehensive plan a standard
PDCA cycle based on the principles of lean management. Set goals,
measure progress, and Plan, Do, Check and Adjust as needed to
reach your goals and increase the supply of affordable housing for
Clark County's people.

Setting goals, measuring whether you are reaching them, and
adjusting as needed is not asking too much. Please add this simple
commitment to set goals and track progress on affordable housing
into the comprehensive plan, at your October 1 hearing.

Sincerely,

Margaret Hess
Vancouver, WA

Dear Planning Commission and Land Use Staff,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rezoning of the property adjacent to
our neighborhood from single-family residential to multi-family/high-density residential.

While a low-density single-family layout along 139th Street represents a manageable expansion
but still not ideal, transitioning this parcel to multi-family apartments presents significant safety,
infrastructure, and environmental challenges:

Traffic & Public Safety: NE 50th Avenue currently experiences heavy traffic volumes and
persistent speeding. Furthermore, Corbin Road serves as a primary access route to I-205. Adding
the vehicle volume of an apartment complex to these corridors will severely compound existing
congestion and substantially elevate collision risks at key intersections.

Environmental Impact & Wildlife: The subject property contains established local wildlife habitat.
High-density development and the accompanying loss of permeable green space will disrupt
these local animal populations and increase stormwater runoff challenges.

Neighborhood Compatibility: A high-density apartment development is incompatible with the
scale, density, and character of the surrounding single-family residential neighborhood.

I respectfully urge the Planning Commission to reject this requested zone change

On behalf of the City of Battle Ground, we appreciate the opportunity to provide the
following comments and recommendations regarding the Comprehensive Plan Update
and Preferred Alternative. Battle Ground has undertaken a multi-year planning process to
evaluate its long-term growth needs, land capacity, infrastructure, and community
priorities. The information and analysis summarized in this letter are intended to provide
the County Council with the City’s perspective and the planning basis for its recommended
growth strategy.
The City Battle Ground concurs with Clark County Planning Commission’s September
3, 2026 recommendation to approve map recommendations 1, 2, and 3, along with
minor amendments 26 and 27, as noted in the decision-making table below.




1|Page
This letter provides a summary of the City of Battle Ground’s goals and recommendations
for the periodic review update. It also addresses the Washington State Department of
Commerce letter directed to Chair Marshall, dated September 9, 2026 (draft) and
September 22, 2026 (final).

The City was not provided with a copy of the Department of Commerce letter when it was
initially distributed to other jurisdictions for review and comment. City staff first became
aware of the letter on September 25, 2026. As a result, Battle Ground has had a limited
opportunity to review and respond to the State’s comments compared with other
jurisdictions whose comments are currently included in the Record. Notwithstanding the
abbreviated timeframe, the City has carefully reviewed the State’s comments and is
providing the information below to clarify the basis for Battle Ground’s proposed
amendments and the planning, analysis, and review that have informed the City’s
recommendations.

Battle Ground’s multi-year Planning Strategy
One of Battle Ground’s primary goals in this periodic review is to expand its Urban Growth
Area (UGA) to the Dollars Corner area to accommodate future employment growth. This
proposal is the culmination of a long-term vision and multi-year planning strategy that
began more than 25 years ago.

2000 – Establishing a 50-Year Vision. In the summer of 2000, the City of Battle Ground
initiated a community visioning process that resulted in the “50 Year Vision for the City of
Battle Ground, Washington.” The vision included a conceptual growth map showing Battle
Ground growing to the west and south. Its guiding principle stated: “Future growth should
occur primarily to the west and south and will occur in all directions consistent with the 50-
year vision.”

2015 – Initial UGA Expansion Request. During the City’s 2015 periodic update, Battle
Ground proposed an 82-acre UGA expansion west of the City, toward the Dollars Corner
area, to accommodate employment growth. The request was challenged before the
Growth Management Hearings Board on appeal (Case No. 16-20005c). The Hearings Board
found that the City’s existing UGA contained a surplus of residential land and raised
questions regarding the City’s density calculations. Although Battle Ground’s proposal
was focused on employment land, the City ultimately chose to withdraw the UGA
expansion request and use the next periodic review cycle to further evaluate the plan for its
employment land needs.

2018–Present – A Deliberate, Multi-Year Planning Strategy. In 2018, Battle Ground
began multi-year planning strategy to more comprehensively evaluate the City’s future
growth needs and establish a foundation for the next periodic review. The City initiated a
community visioning exercise designed to chart a direction for Battle Ground’s future. A
group of citizen volunteers, known as the Navigators, helped guide this effort and develop a
shared vision for the community.


2|Page
  The resulting City Vision and Strategic Action Plan was adopted in 2019 and identified
  several planning efforts necessary to implement that vision, including:
   Land Use Master Plan (2021)
      Shoreline Master Plan Update (2021)
      Housing Action Plan (2021)
      Transportation System Plan (2021) (Updated 2026)
      Parks, Recreation, Open Space Plan (2022)
  These plans provided the City with updated information, community input, policy
  direction, and technical analysis to inform decisions about future growth. As illustrated in
  the Pyramid Action Items below, these individual planning efforts were intended to build
  upon one another and ultimately inform the City’s Comprehensive Plan periodic review.
  The proposed UGA expansion to the Dollars Corner area is therefore not a stand-alone
  request, but the next step in a long-term planning process that has been underway for
  decades.


  Pyramid Action Items

2025 - Current
(Periodic
Review)




2021
Land Use
Master Plan


2018




  Land Use Master Plan
  The Land Use Master Plan (2021) is a foundational planning document supporting Battle
  Ground’s UGA expansion. The plan provides the technical analysis necessary to evaluate
  the City’s land capacity and ability to accommodate projected residential and employment
  growth consistent with the Growth Management Act (GMA), including RCW 36.70A.115. As
  part of this work, the City completed an extensive land capacity analysis, including an
  3|Page
evaluation of the “reasonable measures” available to address identified capacity needs
(RCW 36.70A.215). A key finding was that Battle Ground had approximately 80 acres of net
developable light industrial land available to accommodate future employment growth.
The analysis demonstrated that the City’s existing land supply would not provide sufficient
capacity to meet its employment growth targets without additional land.

The Land Use Master Plan therefore identified the need to consider additional employment
land as part of the City’s long-term growth strategy. The proposed UGA expansion toward
the Dollars Corner area is intended to address this identified need and provide additional
capacity for employment growth. Providing adequate employment capacity also supports
the City’s broader goals of creating opportunities for jobs closer to where residents live,
reducing the need for longer commutes, and supporting more efficient patterns of growth.
The Land Use Master Plan, along with the City’s other supporting planning documents and
technical analyses, is included in the Record for consideration in this decision-making
process.

The Land Use Master Plan and other supporting plans are included in the Record in this
decision-making process via the City’s box link available here:
https://cityofbg.box.com/s/gsvfmsvjc5oquz6yiooqvrsgoivujtnk

Battle Ground’s Preferred Growth Alternative
The proposed UGA adjustments are primarily intended to provide additional capacity for
employment growth while maintaining sufficient capacity to accommodate the City’s
residential growth allocation.

The Preferred Alternative expands the UGA west toward the Dollars Corner area by
approximately 450 gross acres. This expansion would bring the existing commercial center
into the UGA and provide additional land to accommodate future employment growth. The
area has already benefited from state investment in transportation infrastructure,
providing an established location for future employment and commercial development. Its
location also provides an opportunity to accommodate commercial, freight, and shipping
activity outside of Battle Ground’s central city area.

The Preferred Alternative also removes approximately 330 gross acres in the Meadow
Glade area from the current UGA. Based on existing development patterns, infrastructure
availability, and the City’s analysis of development potential, this area is not anticipated to
develop within the 20-year planning horizon. Removing this area from the UGA allows the
City to focus future residential growth within areas that are more suitable and capable of
accommodating development and associated infrastructure.

Taken together, these adjustments reflect a more focused approach to future growth -
adding land where the City has identified a need for employment capacity while refining
the UGA boundary in areas where development is less likely to occur during the planning
horizon.




4|Page
Land Capacity Analysis
The City’s Land Use Master Plan, refined through the periodic review process, includes a
comprehensive land capacity analysis evaluating the City’s ability to accommodate its
assigned growth. Based on this analysis, Battle Ground demonstrates sufficient capacity
to accommodate approximately 8,056 housing units and 8,594 jobs over the 2025–2045
planning horizon.

This analysis provides the basis for the City’s conclusion that the Preferred Alternative can
accommodate the City’s assigned residential and employment growth while supporting a
more efficient and intentional pattern of future development.




Preferred Alternative Growth Map
Battle Ground’s Preferred Alternative is shown on the following page. In addition to the
proposed UGA adjustments described above, the Preferred Alternative includes two minor
amendments requested by the City to address infrastructure and utility needs. These
amendments were supported in the Clark County Planning Commission’s September 3,
2026 recommendation.

It is important to note that the Battle Ground maps included in the Clark County Council
packet do not reflect the Clark County Planning Commission’s September 3

adjustments are provided in Attachment A of this letter.

Dear County Councilors,

Affordable housing is an emergency and needs to be treated like the crisis it is.
During your public hearing on October 1, please add a commitment to set affordable
housing goals, track progress, and adjust as needed, using the data already being
provided to the county by the state under SB 5587, which passed in 2025.

Setting goals, tracking progress, and adjusting as needed is fundamental for
responsible management toward any goal, and affordable housing certainly deserves
this level of seriousness and focus. Failing to set goals and track whether you are
meeting them indicates a lack of seriousness regarding the affordable housing crisis
that impacts so many Clark County families.

On October 1, please establish in the comprehensive plan a standard PDCA cycle
based on the principles of lean management. Set goals, measure progress, and Plan,
Do, Check and Adjust as needed to reach your goals and increase the supply of
affordable housing for Clark County's people.

Setting goals, measuring whether you are reaching them, and adjusting as needed is
not asking too much. Please add this simple commitment to set goals and track
progress on affordable housing into the comprehensive plan, at your October 1
hearing.

Sincerely,
Amy Mesick

Letter of Support and Recommendations
Clark Communities Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee

September 22, 2026

Clark County Council
1300 Franklin Street, 6th Floor, Vancouver, Washington

Subject: Support for Clark County Comprehensive Growth Plan Update


Dear Members of the Clark County Council,

On behalf of the Clark Communities Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee (BPAC), we appreciate
the opportunity to comment on the Transportation Element and Transportation Capital Facility Plan
(CFP) of the County’s Comprehensive Growth Plan update.

We urge this Council to see the wisdom of prioritizing active transportation in Clark County’s long-term
transportation strategy. Active transportation is any means of transportation not in a motor vehicle – it
is human-powered or electrically assisted, for example biking, walking, wheelchair, scooter, etc.

This Comprehensive Growth Plan update provides an important opportunity to establish that
commitment.

Why make active transportation a strategic priority?

Active transportation is cheaper to build than car-centric roadwork. It pays for itself through health and
safety savings. It attracts businesses and increases property values. It makes a place better to live in with
lower-cost options to run local errands, as well as getting to nearby schools, shopping and places of
employment. Active transportation also contributes to the County’s goal in the Comprehensive Plan to have
net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

We have already invested in part of the network. We now must connect the parts, and correct safety issues.
Here is an opportunity to commit to a complete and connected active transportation system. The $490
million estimated cost of all active transportation projects for the next 20 years represents the fact that the
county has not in the past prioritized active transportation. The listed projects address problem areas that
have existed for a long time, more than 16 years in many cases. It’s time to pick up the pace by implementing
the fixes. If we continue to pass the buck, these costs will escalate. In addition, it is more expensive to
retrofit after the fact than to build truly useful active transportation facilities as development occurs.

BPAC recommends the following actions this council should take in the Comprehensive Growth Plan Update.




DRAFT
For other –  09/15/2026
          formats, contact the Clark County ADA Office: 564.397.2322 / 711 or 800.833.6388 / ADA@clark.wa.gov
Adopt the Proposed Multimodal Level of Service Standards

BPAC support the adoption of the multimodal levels of service (MMLOS) standards for active transportation
facilities that are proposed in the Comprehensive Plan’s Transportation Element, including Level of Traffic
Stress (LTS) 2 (meaning Low level of traffic stress; comfortable for most adults) or better for facilities within
the unincorporated Vancouver Urban Growth Area (VUGA) and LTS 3 (meaning Medium level of traffic
stress; tolerable for enthusiastic and/or confident adults) or better for facilities in the rural areas, outside the
VUGA, for corridors identified in the Southwest Washington Regional Transportation Council’s (RTC)
Regional Active Transportation
Network.

Without this standard the network will continue to lack safety and connectivity. If multimodal transportation
is to be part of Clark County’s future, our development code must clearly define what multimodal
infrastructure should look like. The current code primarily provides guidance for a six-foot bike lane as a
universal solution, which is not sufficient for a safe and connected network for all.

Different roadways and contexts require different treatment types, as the LTS framework MMLOS specifies.
Appropriate facilities may include protected bike lanes, buffered bike lanes, shared-use paths, and other
context-sensitive designs. To successfully implement the projects identified in the Capital Facilities Plan, the
County needs clear design standards and guidance for the range of active transportation facilities identified in
the draft Comprehensive Plan.

The Growth Management Act provides an opportunity to plan for safer, lower-stress connections that are
comfortable for a broader range of users, including families, children, older adults, and new riders. These
facilities align well with the proposed Multimodal Level of Stress standard in the Transportation Element.

Adopt the Transportation Element’s Active Transportation Component

We support the adoption of the updated Active Transportation Component of the Comprehensive Growth
Plan Update Chapter 5: Transportation element. In response to the GMA’s new requirements related to
active transportation, BPAC worked with and advised county staff on updating the required active
transportation component through the development of a proposed active transportation network. The
proposed network builds off the 2010 Bicycle and Pedestrian Master Plan and ensures consistency with the
new proposed MMLOS standards.

Address the Pace and Priority of Active Transportation Projects

Although a few active transportation projects have been implemented thus far, we recommend that the
selection criteria for Public Works capital projects be revised to increase the pace at which bicycle and
pedestrian improvements are delivered. Completing one or two projects each year for the next 20 years is
not sufficient to address the substantial gaps that currently exist (described in the 150 listed projects).

The County needs a deliberate investment strategy focused on closing existing gaps, addressing dangerous
conditions, and creating a network that is safe and useful for the average person—not just experienced users.
BPAC supports the recommended Active Transportation Plan in the CFP (Appendix A, pg. 14) as an additional
planning effort to follow the Comprehensive Plan that would provide an update to the 2010 Clark County
Bicycle and Pedestrian Master Plan. This effort would include updating the local active transportation
network, policy framework, project prioritization, and the development of a five-year implementation
strategy.

BPAC is offering its assistance in the large task of ranking priorities of each active transportation project. We
have already given input to the draft Transportation Capital Facility Plan Evaluation Criteria, and the
committee can further help provide a current view of community needs by engaging with residents,
neighborhood groups, businesses, transportation advocates, and other partners. This would help to identify
current priorities and ensure that projects reflect real-world needs. Community engagement can also cover
other issues at the same time which may help to clarify questions such as preference of funding options.
BPAC is committed to being your partner and your agent in this process. We intend to bring a plan to Council
for consideration in the near future.

A Practical Investment in Our Future

The County’s 20-year capital transportation projections make clear that resources will be constrained. That
reality makes prioritization more important, not less. Active transportation infrastructure can provide
significant transportation value at a fraction of the cost of major roadway expansion. A safe sidewalk,
protected bicycle facility, or shared-use path can provide residents with practical options for reaching parks,
schools, businesses, transit stops, and nearby destinations without relying on a vehicle.

The barriers that prevent people from choosing these options today are largely the result of past investment
decisions. Clark County has not yet built a sufficiently safe, connected, and convenient active transportation
network. That can change. Prioritizing active transportation can help reduce congestion, improve air quality,
lower transportation-related carbon emissions, and support healthier communities.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Comprehensive Growth Plan update. We encourage the
Council to use this process to establish active transportation as a clear and sustained priority for Clark
County.

In alignment with the Clark County Bicycle and Pedestrian Master Plan (2010), BPAC supports the County’s
goals of GHG reduction, VMT reduction and net-zero target by 2050. Active transportation could help as a
strategy with achieving some of these goals and required benchmarks. We have diligently worked to perform
committee responsibilities and hope the input and recommendations are helpful to Council as you weight
these decisions:

    •   BPAC provided input on the Transportation Element's goals and policies in the Fall of 2024.
    •   BPAC formally recommended the "Bicycle Facility Typology" (8/05/2025) that has been incorporated
        in the Transportation Element’s required active transportation component.
    •   BPAC provided input on and a formal recommendation (12/16/2025) to APPROVE the proposed
        Multimodal Level of Service standards.
    •   BPAC provided input on and a formal recommendation (6/23/2026) to APPROVE the proposed
        Active Transportation Network to serve as the Transportation Element’s updated active
        transportation component.
    •   BPAC provided input on and formal recommendation (6/23/2026) to APPROVE the draft CFP
        Evaluation Criteria used to prioritize improvement projects.
    •   BPAC provided input on and a formal recommendation (6/23/2026) to APPROVE the draft CFP
        Project List.



Sincerely,




David Zilavy, Chair
Clark Communities Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee

Message Subject
Re-zoning

Comments
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rezoning near NE 50th Ave and NE 139th St from R1-
7.5 to R32/R36.

This is not a minor zoning adjustment. It would allow a substantial increase in residential density
in an area that is currently made up largely of lower-density neighborhoods, larger residential
properties, and open land. The change would fundamentally alter the development pattern and
character of this part of the community.

My primary concern is infrastructure. NE 50th Ave, NE 139th St, and the surrounding road network
were not designed around apartment-scale residential density. A major increase in the number of
households in this area would also increase vehicle trips through the same roads and
intersections that existing residents rely on every day.

Before approving this rezoning, the County should demonstrate that the transportation system
can support the maximum amount of development the new zoning would permit, not just a
hypothetical first project. That analysis should address traffic volumes, intersection capacity,
emergency access, pedestrian and bicycle safety, school traffic, and the cumulative effect of
future development throughout the surrounding area.
There are only two realistic outcomes if the current roads cannot support the additional density.
Either residents will be left with significantly more congestion on the existing road network, or the
County will eventually need to widen roads, rebuild intersections, add signals, acquire right-of-
way, or undertake other major transportation projects to accommodate the growth created by the
rezoning.

The second outcome is not impact-free. Major road expansion could mean years of construction
near existing homes, construction noise, traffic detours, reduced access, loss of roadside space,
and potentially right-of-way impacts to neighboring properties.. Existing residents should not be
forced to choose between worsening congestion and years of disruptive infrastructure
construction because land was rezoned for a level of density the area was not prepared to
support.

I am also concerned about compatibility with the surrounding neighborhoods. Moving directly
from R1-7.5 to R32/R36 is a major increase in development intensity. Large multifamily projects
can create substantial changes in building scale, traffic, parking demand, lighting, noise, privacy,
and overall activity. If the County believes additional density is appropriate in this broader area,
there should be a thoughtful transition in density rather than placing high-density multifamily
zoning directly next to established lower-density neighborhoods and semi-rural properties.

I recognize that Clark County must plan for population growth and additional housing. My
objection is not to housing or multifamily housing in general. It is to concentrating a significant
amount of new density in a location without first showing that the surrounding transportation
network, utilities, schools, emergency services, stormwater systems, and other public
infrastructure can reasonably support it.

Before approving this change, I ask the County to clearly answer the following questions:

How many additional housing units could ultimately be built in this area under R32/R36 zoning
compared with the existing R1-7.5 zoning?

How many additional daily vehicle trips could result at full buildout?

What would be the projected impact on NE 50th Ave, NE 139th St, and nearby intersections?

Would road widening, intersection reconstruction, new signals, or additional right-of-way be
required?

If so, when would those improvements occur, how long would construction last, and how would
they be funded?

What measures would protect adjacent lower-density neighborhoods from abrupt changes in
building scale, traffic, lighting, noise, and privacy?
What evidence shows that the necessary infrastructure will be in place before, rather than after,
this additional development occurs?

Rezoning should follow adequate infrastructure planning. It should not create a situation where
the County approves significantly greater density first and then asks existing residents to absorb
the congestion, construction, and other consequences afterward.

For these reasons, I strongly urge the County to reject the proposed R32/R36 rezoning near NE
50th Ave and NE 139th St and retain the existing lower-density zoning. At minimum, the County
should require a lower-density transition area and complete a site-specific transportation and
infrastructure analysis before allowing such a substantial increase in development intensity.

Thank you for considering the concerns of the residents who live in and have invested in this
community.

On to the rest...

We are writing to you again in collaboration as a coalition of individuals and
organizations including: Green Party of Southwest Washington, Southwest Washington
Equity Coalition, Southwest Washington LULAC, Vietnamese Community of Clark
County, Hispanic Disability Support SWWA (Pasitos Gigantes), Sierra Club Loowit
Group, Western Institute for Agriculture and Food Security Foundation, Pacific Islander
Community Association of WA (PICAWA), iUrban Teen, Vancouver Metro LULAC Council
47026, Columbia Riverkeeper, Vancouver Audubon Society, SW WA Victory Food
Project, Fourth Plain Forward, Alliance for Community Engagement (ACE), and Cycle
Vancouver. We are writing to strongly urge you to adopt greenhouse gas (GHG)
emissions reduction targets aligned with the City of Vancouver’s reduction targets and
to draft a supplemental EIS that creates a viable alternative through appropriate up-
zoning that limits urban growth boundary (UGB) expansion and protects agricultural
resource lands in the 2025 Clark County Comprehensive Plan Update (Comp Plan
Update).
Align greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets with the City of Vancouver’s
reduction targets.

According to Community Planning staff, the currently proposed GHG emissions
reduction targets for unincorporated Clark County within the Comp Plan Update Climate
Element Draft are insufficient and create risk in meeting the statewide 2050 target
established in RCW 70A.45.020. Unincorporated Clark County and the City of Vancouver
account for 84% of Clark County GHG emissions, 40% and 44% respectively. Adopting
the City of Vancouver’s targets of 80% reduction in GHG emissions by 2030 and carbon
neutrality by 2040 would align with the responses of a majority of the Clark County
Climate Advisory Group and reflect the bold leadership and sense of urgency necessary
to address our rapidly accelerating climate emergency.

As noted by staff, a significant portion of Clark County GHG emissions are produced by
sources like transportation (36% of total emissions) and agriculture and tree loss (21%)
which are out of County control. We strongly agree that establishing more ambitious
reduction targets could create the necessary sense of urgency and innovation while
allowing more time to adapt further if the County falls short of interim goals.
Additionally, by adopting reduction targets aligned with the City of Vancouver, the
County could model strong leadership on addressing climate change as Washougal,
Ridgefield, and Camas--which has a high 2022 GHG emissions baseline--align on their
own reduction targets in the near future. As a reminder, there is no penalty for missing
more ambitious targets. However, Clark County has the opportunity to work alongside
the City of Vancouver in reducing our carbon footprint and providing environmental and
public health benefits for the majority of residents sooner.

No expansion of UGBs or de-designation of agricultural resource lands.

Additionally, we would like to echo the sentiment of the majority of prior written public
comment and verbal testimony for the Preferred Alternative hearing in April, and
FutureWise’s public comment dated July 30, 2026, regarding the expansion of UGBs and
de-designation of agricultural resource lands protected by the Growth Management Act.
Reducing urban sprawl by accommodating projected housing and employment targets
within existing urban growth areas through appropriate up-zoning and development
could help reduce vehicle miles traveled and associated GHG emissions. Additionally,
we strongly believe that in order to meet the goal of “promot[ing] holistic and resilient
food economies” to expand local food security as stated in the Chapter 14 Climate
Element draft, legally protected agricultural resource lands should not be de-
designated. As accelerating climate change increases surface air temperatures, the
frequency of extreme weather events, and threatens crop yields and the stability of the
global food system, our reliance on our local food system will become more important
than ever. As it was stated in public testimony at the Preferred Alternative Hearing, “we
cannot eat concrete.”

We would also like to specifically highlight the Washington Department of Commerce’s
recent letter to the Council dated September 22nd, 2026, which reinforces our
understanding that the Vacant Buildable Lands Model indicates that the current UGBs
are sufficient to accommodate projected growth. Additionally, we agree with Commerce
that the County has not clearly identified “insufficient capacity for housing needs,
document[ed] how they have evaluated zoning changes to accommodate deficits in
housing capacity, and then document[ed] sufficient capacity with any UGA changes
after these previous steps.” Regarding a Transfer of Development Rights Program (Policy
1.1.24), Commerce is clear that “TDR programs are not intended to be used as a
mechanism to expand UGA Boundaries.” We also strongly believe that TDRs should not
be used to facilitate the de-designation and destruction of protected agricultural lands.
Additionally, TDRs should not be used to essentially leverage a loophole to designate
and transfer development rights of lands that should have already been designated and
protected based on the 2025 Clark County Agricultural Lands Study. Further, Commerce
is clear that the de-designation of agricultural resource lands has “historically has not
been found to be defensible by the Growth Management Hearings Board.”

Draft a supplemental EIS with appropriate up-zoning to accommodate housing and
employment targets.

We are again urging you to do the right thing and call for a supplemental EIS (WAC 197-
11-405) leveraging the Vacant Buildable Lands Model data to create a viable alternative
with appropriate up-zoning that omits or greatly reduces UGB expansion, ideally
eliminating the de-designation of valuable agricultural resource lands which are
protected by the Growth Management Act and critical to safeguarding our local food
system.

To be clear, we are not anti-development. We are simply calling for appropriate and
responsible development, aligned with the intent of, and in compliance with, the Growth
Management Act. Clark County is a beautiful place blessed with abundant resources
including prime soils for farming. We are confident that our County leaders are capable
of drafting an alternative and Comp Plan Update that will accommodate the need for
housing and employing new neighbors while also protecting our resources and food
security.
It is not too late. Will you join us in protecting Clark County?

We are writing to you today because we believe in democracy and your commitment as
elected representatives of the people to not only listen to our community but act on our
behalf. Our community is clearly expressing that we do not consent to a bare minimum
approach to climate action, expansion of urban growth areas and increasing urban
sprawl, and the destruction of our precious agricultural resource lands and
jeopardization of our future food security--for ourselves, our children, and future
generations. While we recognize that our level of climate concern may be different than
yours, we would like to remind you that our youth are growing up in a vastly different
world. Climate anxiety among youth is a significant and growing concern and can be
seen in kids as young as three years old. Committing to bold climate action and
protecting our resources and food security is in service of our children’s and future
generation’s physical and mental health. Therefore, we are urging you to stand with us--
not only as our elected representatives and fellow Clark County residents and
neighbors--but also as fellow parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles. Your decision in this
moment will impact generations to come. Let’s act together as responsible stewards of
our community and this land to protect them for future generations.

Message Subject
Pro ag land; pro climate action; anti UGA expansion

Comments
Dear Councilors,

I am a rural resident of Battle Ground and a former small farmer who sold produce at the Battle
Ground and Salmon Creek farmers markets. I depended on a strong local food culture to support
my family, and I am writing to urge you to make three commitments in the Comprehensive Plan
Update: no Urban Growth Area expansions, no de-designation of agricultural land, and
meaningful climate action.

First, the county's own analysis shows expansion isn't needed. The Final Environmental Impact
Statement acknowledges that the Preferred Alternative exceeds the land capacity required for the
housing and job growth projected over the next 20 years. The Washington Department of
Commerce reached a similar conclusion, noting that current urban growth area boundaries
appear sufficient and that the county has not shown how it would provide urban services to
expanded areas. Commerce also found no clear demonstration that lands proposed for de-
designation no longer meet the criteria for agricultural designation, and warned that de-
designating farmland based mainly on its proximity to urban growth has historically not held up
before the Growth Management Hearings Board.

Second, the land at stake is irreplaceable, and my neighbors and I are already watching it
disappear. Agricultural land around Battle Ground is being rezoned and developed at a rapid pace
as suburban growth accelerates. The new warehouse on 50th near WSUV demonstrates what
poor planning looks like: damaged roads, disrupted neighborhoods, and public comment that
was disregarded. The expansions requested by Ridgefield, La Center, and Camas would cover
hundreds of acres of prime agricultural soils and farmlands of statewide importance, and Battle
Ground's proposal would do the same to ag-quality rural land identified in the county's own
Agricultural Lands Study. Using nearby development as a reason to de-designate farmland only
invites more development, a cycle your own county counsel has described as "the absolute
definition of urban sprawl." The Agricultural Advisory Commission voted to keep all existing
agricultural designations, and I hope you will honor their recommendation.

Third, this plan must include meaningful climate action. Farmland supports local food security
and climate resilience, and the recommendations of the Climate Community Advisory Group will
have little effect without an explicit greenhouse gas reduction goal. I urge the county to match the
City of Vancouver's emissions goals.

Our residents need housing and jobs, but they also need food, clean water, and natural spaces.
Please weigh the needs of the whole county rather than reward cities for proposing growth that
relies on developing farmland. Please, keep our urban growth boundaries where they are, keep
agricultural designations intact, and adopt real climate goals.

Thank you for your time and service.

opposition to the proposed zoning changes being considered as part of the 2025–2045
Comprehensive Plan Update.

As a homeowner who will be directly affected by decisions regarding increased residential
density, I am concerned about how these changes could alter the character and quality of life in
established residential neighborhoods. I purchased my home in this area in part because of the
peace, quiet, and residential environment it provides, and I believe those interests should be
considered when evaluating significant increases in density.

My home is located on a corner lot along a two-way residential street. Increased density and the
addition of substantially more housing in the surrounding area could mean more vehicles
traveling through neighborhood streets, increased parking demand, additional congestion, and
greater pedestrian and vehicle activity immediately around existing homes.

Noise is also a significant concern. Higher residential density can bring increased vehicle traffic,
deliveries, construction activity, and general activity associated with a larger number of residents
in a concentrated area. For homeowners who purchased property in an established lower-density
neighborhood, these changes could affect the quiet residential environment we currently
experience.

I also believe the County should clearly explain how allowing substantially more apartment and
higher-density development is expected to address housing affordability. If apartments are
already available in the broader area but remain unaffordable to many of the households
experiencing housing insecurity or cost burdens, simply increasing the number of units does not
by itself demonstrate that those households will be able to afford them. What portion of the
additional housing anticipated under these zoning changes is expected to be affordable to the
residents the County is seeking to help, and at what income levels?

Before changing established neighborhoods to accommodate substantially greater density,
residents deserve to understand the expected benefit and the evidence supporting it. I
respectfully ask the County to provide information showing how the proposed zoning changes are
expected to improve housing affordability, rather than relying solely on an increase in overall
housing supply.

I am also concerned about whether existing infrastructure and public services are prepared to
accommodate substantial additional development. Before approving zoning changes that could
increase the number of residents and housing units in these areas, I respectfully ask the County
to carefully evaluate road capacity, traffic impacts, schools, utilities, emergency services, public-
safety service demand, parking, and other infrastructure needs.

I understand that communities grow and housing needs change. However, growth should be
thoughtfully planned and balanced against its effects on the people who already live in these
neighborhoods. Existing homeowners and residents made significant financial and personal
decisions based, in part, on the characteristics of the communities in which they chose to live.

I respectfully ask the County Council to carefully consider these impacts and the concerns of
residents and property owners who will be directly affected before approving significant increases
in residential density.

Please include my comments as part of the official public record regarding the 2025–2045
Comprehensive Plan Update.

Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,

Ileana Stover

Karissa Halstrom

Sent with Proton Mail secure email.
September 30, 2026

Clark County Council
PO Box 5000
Vancouver, WA 98666

Dear Chair Marshall, and Councilors Belkot, Fuentes, Little, and Yung,

We are writing to you again in collaboration as a coalition of 61 individuals and 17
organizations including: iUrban Teen, WSU Vancouver Environmental Science Club, Southwest
Washington Equity Coalition, Fourth Plain Forward, Southwest Washington LULAC, Vancouver
Metro LULAC Council 47026, Vietnamese Community of Clark County, Hispanic Disability Support
SWWA (Pasitos Gigantes), Pacific Islander Community Association of WA (PICAWA), SW WA
Victory Food Project, Western Institute for Agriculture and Food Security Foundation, Columbia
Riverkeeper, Vancouver Audubon Society, Sierra Club Loowit Group, Cycle Vancouver, Alliance for
Community Engagement (ACE), and Green Party of Southwest Washington.

We are writing to strongly urge you to adopt greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction
targets aligned with the City of Vancouver's reduction targets and to draft a supplemental
EIS that creates a viable alternative through appropriate up-zoning that limits urban growth
boundary (UGB) expansion and protects agricultural resource lands in the 2025 Clark County
Comprehensive Plan Update (Comp Plan Update).

1. Align greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets with the City of Vancouver's
  reduction targets.

According to Community Planning staff, the currently proposed GHG emissions reduction targets
for unincorporated Clark County within the Comp Plan Update Climate Element Draft are
insufficient and create risk in meeting the statewide 2050 target established in RCW 70A.45.020.
Unincorporated Clark County and the City of Vancouver account for 84% of Clark County GHG
emissions, 40% and 44% respectively. Adopting the City of Vancouver's targets of 80% reduction
in GHG emissions by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2040 would align with the responses of a
majority of the Clark County Climate Advisory Group and reflect the bold leadership and sense of
urgency necessary to address our rapidly accelerating climate emergency.

As noted by staff, a significant portion of Clark County GHG emissions are produced by sources
like transportation (36% of total emissions) and agriculture and tree loss (21%) which are out of
County control. We strongly agree that establishing more ambitious reduction targets could create
the necessary sense of urgency and innovation while allowing more time to adapt further if the
County falls short of interim goals. Additionally, by adopting reduction targets aligned with the City
of Vancouver, the County could model strong leadership on addressing climate change as
Washougal, Ridgefield, and Camas--which has a high 2022 GHG emissions baseline--align on
their own reduction targets in the near future. As a reminder, there is no penalty for missing more
ambitious targets. However, Clark County has the opportunity to work alongside the City of
Vancouver in reducing our carbon footprint and providing environmental and public health benefits
for the majority of residents sooner.

2. No expansion of UGBs or de-designation of agricultural resource lands.

Additionally, we would like to echo the sentiment of the majority of prior written public comment
and verbal testimony for the Preferred Alternative hearing in April, and FutureWise's public
comment dated July 30, 2026, regarding the expansion of UGBs and de-designation of agricultural
resource lands protected by the Growth Management Act. Reducing urban sprawl by
accommodating projected housing and employment targets within existing urban growth areas
through appropriate up-zoning and development could help reduce vehicle miles traveled and
associated GHG emissions. Additionally, we strongly believe that in order to meet the goal of
"promot[ing] holistic and resilient food economies" to expand local food security as stated in the
Chapter 14 Climate Element draft, legally protected agricultural resource lands should not be de-
designated. As accelerating climate change increases surface air temperatures, the frequency of
extreme weather events, and threatens crop yields and the stability of the global food system, our
reliance on our local food system will become more important than ever. As it was stated in public
testimony at the Preferred Alternative Hearing, "we cannot eat concrete."

We would also like to specifically highlight the Washington Department of Commerce's recent letter
to the Council dated September 22nd, 2026, which reinforces our understanding that the Vacant
Buildable Lands Model indicates that the current UGBs are sufficient to accommodate
projected growth. Additionally, we agree with Commerce that the County has not clearly identified
"insufficient capacity for housing needs, document[ed] how they have evaluated zoning changes to
accommodate deficits in housing capacity, and then document[ed] sufficient capacity with any UGA
changes after these previous steps." Regarding a Transfer of Development Rights Program (Policy
1.1.24), Commerce is clear that "TDR programs are not intended to be used as a mechanism to
expand UGA Boundaries." We also strongly believe that TDRs should not be used to facilitate the
de-designation and destruction of protected agricultural lands. Additionally, TDRs should not be
used to essentially leverage a loophole to designate and transfer development rights of lands that
should have already been designated and protected based on the 2025 Clark County Agricultural
Lands Study. Further, Commerce is clear that the de-designation of agricultural resource lands has
"historically has not been found to be defensible by the Growth Management Hearings Board."

3. Draft a supplemental EIS with appropriate up-zoning to accommodate housing and
  employment targets.

We are again urging you to do the right thing and call for a supplemental EIS (WAC 197-11-405)
leveraging the Vacant Buildable Lands Model data to create a viable alternative with appropriate
up-zoning that omits or greatly reduces UGB expansion, ideally eliminating the de-designation of
valuable agricultural resource lands which are protected by the Growth Management Act and
critical to safeguarding our local food system.

To be clear, we are not anti-development. We are simply calling for appropriate and responsible
development, aligned with the intent of, and in compliance with, the Growth Management Act.
Clark County is a beautiful place blessed with abundant resources including prime soils for
farming. We are confident that our County leaders are capable of drafting an alternative and Comp
Plan Update that will accommodate the need for housing and employing new neighbors while also
protecting our resources and food security.

It is not too late. Will you join us in protecting Clark County?

We are writing to you today because we believe in democracy and your commitment as elected
representatives of the people to not only listen to our community but act on our behalf. Our
community is clearly expressing that we do not consent to a bare minimum approach to
climate action, expansion of urban growth areas and increasing urban sprawl, and the
destruction of our precious agricultural resource lands and jeopardization of our future
food security--for ourselves, our children, and future generations. While we recognize that
our level of climate concern may be different than yours, we would like to remind you that our
youth are growing up in a vastly different world. Climate anxiety among youth is a significant and
growing concern and can be seen in kids as young as three years old. Committing to bold climate
action and protecting our resources and food security is in service of our children's and future
generation's physical and mental health. Therefore, we are urging you to stand with us--not only as
our elected representatives and fellow Clark County residents and neighbors--but also as fellow
parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles. Your decision in this moment will impact generations to
come. Let's act together as responsible stewards of our community and this land to protect them
for future generations.

We, the undersigned 17 organizations and 61 individuals, strongly urge Clark County
Council to adopt greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets aligned with the City of
Vancouver and to draft a supplemental EIS that creates a viable alternative that limits urban
growth boundary (UGB) expansion and protect agricultural resource lands in the 2025 Clark
County Comprehensive Plan Update. We appreciate your thoughtful consideration of this matter.

Brandi Cole, District 2

Karissa Halstrom-Page, District 4

Green Party of Southwest Washington

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the 2025 Comprehensive Plan
Update. Futurewise works throughout Washington State to support land-use
policies that encourage healthy, equitable, and opportunity-rich communities, and
that protect our most valuable farmlands, forests, and water resources.
Futurewise has members and supporters across Washington State including in
Clark County.

Summary of the Recommendations
Futurewise has the following comments and recommendations:
 Futurewise recommends aligning the County’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions
  reduction targets with the City of Vancouver’s reduction targets and to adopt
  policies and regulations consistent with the State of Washington Department of
  Commerce’s Clark County 2022 Greenhouse Gas Emissions Analysis. This is
  necessary to comply with the climate element requirements of the Growth
  Management Act (GMA). Please see page 2 of this letter for more information.
 Because urban area expansions are not needed, the comprehensive plan cannot
  expand the urban growth areas (UGAs). Expanding the UGAs would violate the
  Growth Management Act (GMA). Please see page 4 of this letter for more
  information.
 The UGAs must not be expanded onto agricultural lands of long-term
  commercial significance. This is necessary to comply with the GMA. Please see
  page 4 of this letter for more information.
 Draft a supplemental EIS with appropriate up-zoning to accommodate
  affordable housing targets. While the UGAs have sufficient capacity for housing
Re: Comments on the Comprehensive Plan Update
September 30, 2026
Page 2

    and population, they should add additional affordable housing types. A draft
    supplemental EIS will provide the analysis needed to provide more affordable
    housing within the existing urban growth areas. Please see page 6 of this letter
    for more information.
 Adopt an Agriculture 40 (AG-40) zone to better protect working farms. This
  will help maintain the agricultural industry in the county and to protect access
  to fresh and healthy food. Please see page 7 of this letter for more information.
 Prohibit cluster land divisions in Agriculture zones. Cluster subdivisions do not
  protect farmland; they ultimately reduce the agricultural land base over time.
  Please see page 8 of this letter for more information.

Detailed Recommendations
Align greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reduction targets with the City of
Vancouver’s reduction targets and adopt policies and regulations consistent
with Commerce’s Clark County 2022 Greenhouse Gas Emissions Analysis.

RCW 36.70A.020(14) and RCW 36.70A.070(9) provide that “[i]t is up to each
jurisdiction to create a program ‘with a demonstrated ability to reduce emissions’
in a manner which achieves” the state adopted greenhouse gas emission reduction
targets. 1 These targets are in RCW 70A.45.020(1)(a) and (c) and call for net zero
greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. The City of Vancouver calls for a goal that the
city be carbon neutral by 2040 which we certainly support. 2

Either way, the County must comply with RCW 36.70A.070(9)(d)(ii). In the
Thurston County decision analyzing the GMA’s greenhouse gas reduction
requirements, the Growth Management Hearings Board concluded that the
legislature in RCW 36.70A.070(9)(d)(ii) “has directly required” the greenhouse
gas emissions reduction subelement to be consistent with the State of Washington

Thurston County adopted different policies than those recommended by
Commerce. 4 As the Board concluded:

       Here the County did not provide any scientifically credible projection
       analyzing how much GHG emission reduction its adopted policies
       would achieve. In the absence of such analysis, the County had no
       basis to conclude that its adopted policies for GHG emissions
       reduction would be equivalent to or better than those identified by
       Commerce. The County has not calculated the GHG emission
       reductions its policies will achieve. The County did not provide the
       required equivalency analysis and, therefore, failed to meet the
       requirements of RCW 36.70A.070(9)(d)(i). 5

As Futurewise’s Comment Letter to the Clark County Planning Commission (July
30, 2026) documented on pages 10 to 19, Clark County has also not proposed to
adopt the policies recommended by Commerce. We have not been able to find any
scientifically credible projection analyzing how much GHG emission reductions the
Clark County climate policies would achieve. This violates the requirements of
RCW 36.70A.070(9)(d). Further, the scientifically credible projections must also
include greenhouse gas emissions from the urban growth area expansions and
rural, agricultural, and forestry growth projections. Rural residents have
substantially higher greenhouse gas emissions, particularly higher transport-
related direct greenhouse gas emissions, than residents in the urban growth

vast majority of lands identified in the study area are physically well-suited for
agricultural production.” 15 The other factors also show that these lands qualify as
agricultural lands of long-term commercial significance. 16 The Land Use Element
and Future Land Use Map must retain the existing agricultural lands of long-term

The land that Ridgefield and La Center are requesting to pave over forever are
prime agricultural lands and farmlands of statewide importance and meet the
other criteria for agricultural lands of long-term commercial significance. 17
Consequently, these lands cannot be legally dedesignated under WAC 365-190-
040(10)(c). Since the lands cannot be dedesignated legally, they cannot be legally
added to the UGAs unless the land added has been protected for agricultural use
through the adoption of a purchase or transfer of its development rights. 18

In the past Clark County was able to dedesignate agricultural lands of long-term
commercial significance that continued to meet the criteria and have them
annexed before the Growth Management Hearings Board and the courts found that
these dedesignations violated the Growth Management Act. That is no longer
possible because dedesignations and urban growth area expansions do not
take effect until after the Growth Management Hearings Board appeals are
resolved. 19 So, dedesignations that violate state law are now a waste of time
and money as they will be appealed and overturned and cannot be annexed
during the appeal period. 20

affordable housing targets.

provide for more affordable housing types. While the UGAs have sufficient
capacity for housing, population and employment, they should add additional
capacity for affordable housing types. This should include housing affordable to
families earning extremely low incomes (0% to 30% of area median income

The comprehensive plan should better protect agricultural lands of long-term
commercial significance.

The Growth Management Act requires Clark County “to assure the conservation of
agricultural lands and to assure that the use of adjacent lands does not interfere
with their continued use for the production of food or agricultural products. 21
Adopting an Agriculture 40 (AG 40) zone for agricultural lands of long-term
commercial significance and prohibiting cluster subdivisions on agricultural lands
would significantly improve protection for working farms.

Adopt an Agriculture 40 (AG-40) zone to better protect working farms.

Clark County’s BERK report documents that the 20-acre minimum lot size and
non-agricultural uses allowed by the Agriculture (AG-20) comprehensive plan
designation and zone fails to conserve agricultural land of long-term commercial
significance because they allow “non-productive rural uses.” 22 “Given onsite
development or other non-productive rural uses (e.g. dwellings, manicured lawns
associated with dwellings, etc.) there is a greater area zoned AG and a lesser area
inventoried by [the Washington State Department of Agriculture] WSDA in
agricultural use. WSDA inventoried acres make up between 15-27% of the AG 10
zone area [which is now zoned AG-20].” 23 The BERK report also found based on the
Census of Agriculture that “1.5% of the [Clark County] farms are large,
representing 72% of the total commodity outputs. … The loss of large farms
corresponds to a loss in commodity totals. In 2007 dollars, the value of agriculture
dropped from $62.3 million in 1997 to $52.7 million in 2007, and again to $45.9
million in 2012.” 24 Converting large farms to small farms and 20-acre estates with

Prohibit cluster land divisions in Agriculture zones.

Clustering is not an effective method of protecting working farms. A peer-
reviewed study of clustering in comparison to other techniques showed that it
does not protect farmland long-term. 26 Clustering because it only protects a
portion of the farmland leads to a reduction in parcel sizes. 27 Smaller parcels can
be difficult to farm long-term. “Contiguity with other protected land can be an
important factor in the long-term farming status of a particular parcel of land.” 28
Cluster programs cannot maintain continuity with other protected land and can

lead to situations where farmland is located close or even surrounded by

          The most significant weakness in the cluster program is the issue of
          preservation of the agricultural land base: only 6% of the original
          agricultural land base has been protected through the use of
          clustering, and only an average of 36% of an original parcel is
          protected under the requirements of the program. Thus, the effect of
          the cluster program is increasing fragmentation and loss of the land
          base. 30

As this peer-reviewed study shows, cluster subdivisions will not maintain the
agricultural land base in Clark County. Cluster subdivisions should not be allowed
on agricultural lands of long-term commercial significance.

     Reviewer Guidelines
     Manuscripts submitted to the American Economic Review are reviewed in a single-blind
     fashion. Because the referee(s) should remain anonymous to authors, we ask you not to
     use your name in the body or filename of your report.

     All manuscript submissions are accompanied by individual disclosure statements from
     each coauthor. However, recommendations should not be based on whether potential
     conflicts of interest exist, but on whether the conclusions in the paper are robust,
     credible, and worthy of publication.

     The AEA uses ScholarOne Manuscripts for submission and peer review tracking. To
     see more information and instructions for submitting a review, log in and navigate to
     your Reviewer Center.

     We encourage you to read the brief set of guidelines on referee reports prepared by
     Econometrica and the more detailed guidelines published in the Journal of Economic
     Perspectives by Jonathan Berk, Campbell Harvey, and David Hirshleifer. These

 Agricultural land fragmentation: the spatial effects of three land
         protection strategies in the eastern United States
                                         Elizabeth Brabeca,*, Chip Smithb
                  a
                   School of Natural Resources and Environment, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48107, USA
                                b
                                  Land Ethics Inc., 201 E. Liberty, Suite 16, Ann Arbor, MI 48104, USA



Abstract

   Fragmentation of agricultural land by urban sprawl affects both the agricultural production capacity of the land and its rural
scenic quality. In order to assess the resulting fragmentation of the three most common types of agricultural land conservation
tools in the United States, this study analyzes the spatial form of three land protection strategies: a purchase of development
rights (PDR) program, a clustering program and a transfer of development rights program. By assessing a series of measures of
success such as total acreage protected, size of parcels, contiguity and farming status, the study compares the effectiveness of
programs that have been in place for approximately 20 years, analyzing the extent to which each program prevents or enhances
fragmentation. The analysis shows that although the number of acres protected is an important factor in program success, the
amount of protected land remaining in active farming is additionally influenced by any development rights that may remain
with the land, the use of a variety of tools to reduce the likelihood of parcel isolation, and the adjacency and contiguity of
protected parcels. # 2002 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

Keywords: Land conservation; Agriculture; Land protection; Metropolitan agriculture; Fragmentation; Urban sprawl

of greenhouse gas emissions within a city region

H I G H L I G H T S

 Household survey data and GPS-veriﬁed travel data are used to estimate GHG emissions.
 Residential location impacts both transportation and housing-related GHG emissions.
 Results reveal spatial variability in direct GHG emissions at the sub-regional scale.
 No signiﬁcant difference in total direct GHG emissions between urban and suburban respondents.
 Travel related GHG emissions are signiﬁcantly higher among those living in the exurbs.




art ic l e i nf o                                        a b s t r a c t

Article history:                                         This research investigates whether where we live matters in terms of contributions to direct greenhouse
Received 26 June 2012                                    gas (GHG) emissions. Using results from the Halifax Space Time Activity Research (STAR) project, we
Accepted 6 July 2013                                     estimate GHG emissions for 1920 randomly selected respondents in Halifax Regional Municipality, Nova
Available online 9 August 2013
                                                         Scotia, Canada. The unique data set allows us to report direct GHG emissions with an unprecedented level
Keywords:                                                of speciﬁcity at the sub-regional scale using household energy-use survey data and GPS-veriﬁed travel
Greenhouse gases                                         data. We report results and investigate statistical differences between communities and urban–rural
Transport                                                zones (inner city, suburban, and inner and outer commuter belts). Results reveal considerable spatial
Suburbs                                                  variability in direct GHG emissions across the study area. Our ﬁndings indicate that individuals living in
                                                         the suburbs generate similar amounts of GHG emissions (20.5 kg CO2e person 1 day 1) to those living in
                                                         the inner city (20.2 kg CO2e person 1 day 1), challenging a widely held assumption that living in the
                                                         urban centre is better for sustainability. However, individuals in more rural areas have signiﬁcantly higher
                                                         transport-related GHG emissions than those living in the inner city and suburbs. Our results underscore
                                                         the importance of understanding the spatial distribution of GHG emissions at the sub-regional scale.
