    narrowed this down in 2025 to four large potential VUGA sites where owners had
    submitted site specific residential upzone requests, in hopes that portions of those sites
    could include a commercial component.

    Yet nothing has happened. Supportive commercial or employment zoning was not added in
    the maps studied through the County’s Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) review
    process. None of the City proposals were even listed on the County Planning Commission
    and Council decision tables, so none were discussed. The Commission was told at their last
    deliberations on September 3 that none of the City proposals coincided with sites that were
    on the County decision list, when in fact two are.

     Specific Action Requested:

     •   Include this overall issue as an item in the County decision table for the VUGA, and
         discuss during Council review of decision table items 18 and 23. Number 18 is a
         residential upzone on 44 acres from R1-5 to R-36, where we suggest including a
         commercial component on NE 119th Street. Number 23 is a conversion on 40 acres from
         MX to R-24, where we suggest including a commercial component on NW 164th Street,
         or at least keeping it as MX.
     •   Take some form of action, either designating some supportive zoning now, or directing
         that the issue be examined in 2027 workplans after Comprehensive Plan adoption.


2. Do not significantly roll back proposed minimum multi-family densities in the VUGA
   before the new Comprehensive Plan has had a chance to work, particularly when based
   on incomplete information. Long term planning should involve not just allowing growth,
   but to a degree trying to shape it. A September 3 DEAB letter raises valid and important
   points about the need to consider market feasibility, but in response proposes reducing
   new VUGA minimum density requirements in all multi-family residential and mixed use
   zones by thirty to forty percent from what the FEIS envisioned. Rollbacks of this scope and
   magnitude would likely undercut the legality and affordability of the County Comprehensive
   Plan, and may not fully represent recent development, let alone future development
   anticipated during the planning period. As noted by County staff at the September 16
   workshop, the multi-family zoning subject to the minimum density requirements in
   question constitute a minority of the overall residential land supply but is necessary to
   provide the less costly housing that many local residents need, and that the GMA requires.

    These recommended density reductions, in some zones to as low as 12 units per acre, are
    based on a table focusing on garden apartment developments averaging around 25 units
    per acre, twice as high. These reported averages would be even higher if the sample
    included more non-garden apartment projects such as the Artifact and Kirkland proposals in




Page 2
    central and eastern Vancouver that are located far from downtown and are planned for
    densities of over 80 units per acre. 2

    Beyond concerns about the completeness of the underlying data, as a matter of process we
    recommend against making major areawide changes to the proposed new Comprehensive
    Plan and zoning code before they have had a chance to work, based on late requests whose
    impacts have not had time to be fully analyzed. The DEAB letter suggests a number of
    specific zoning code changes which would benefit from further review. Deferring these to
    the post-adoption period would provide time for that to happen, and time for the market to
    begin to respond to the new density allowances proposed. This is particularly the case in
    areas where pending infrastructure improvements may impact apartment viability, such as
    the Highway 99 Bus Rapid Transit service scheduled to open in 2027.

    Specific Action Requested:

    •    Adopt zoning code standards as proposed, allowing time to fully evaluate proposed
         changes and monitor market conditions.
    •    If minimum density changes are sought now, limit those to a modest reduction in the
         highest density zones from a 40 units per acre minimum to 35 units per acre.
    •    Allow density minimums to be calculated in a way that supports construction 2- and 3-
         bedroom units, as it is in Vancouver.
    •    Do not allow single family and duplex development in all high-density zones provided
         density requirements are met, as this can facilitate a problematic built environment, and
         encourage building low density housing components first, and later seeking rezones or
         code changes when the remainder goes undeveloped.

My name is Bob Johnson and I live in Clark County.

I’m submitting this comment regarding the draft next 20 year Comprehensive Plan being considered by the Clark County
Council.

I am strongly against the plan being considered to allow growth of the urban growth area (UGA) and instead urgently recommending the
Council consider a more strategic plan.

I understand the “easy” path to growth is just expand the growth area which in turn generates a higher tax base which delivers more tax
revenue. Truly strategic growth is more difficult in the early stages, but we all end up with a more sustainable plan. We get urban
growth without environmental destruction. I strongly recommend building inward on the urban environment that already exists but is
today nowhere near being optimized.

The current plan being consider just considers growth for growths sake. It does not take an honest look into the downside of taking the
easy path being considered. For example:

-It is not weighing today’s declining birthrate or the passing of the boomer generation. Within the next 20 years the county’s own
modeling shows our current urban areas have the capacity to accommodate all expected growth.

-The plan will require expensive storm water management requirements

-It will lead to more habitat loss for our important flora and fauna as more urban sprawl further disrupts crucial natural ecosystems

-We will see more long distance traffic as new communities will have to commute back into the urban core

-Carbon capture will decrease as trees are bulldozed and plowed under and covered with asphalt and cement

-We also lose the ability to use and grow are agricultural areas to grow our food

What does strategic, smart growth look like? It uses existing urban areas that are not even close to being fully utilized:

-Smart growth creates compact, walkable communities

-It promotes infill development instead of allowing more poorly utilized sprawl

-It revitalizes existing urban areas

-It minimized transportation distances allowing for shorter commutes, leading to higher quality of life for its inhabitants

-Strategic growth, with more concentrated and well planned existing urban areas will promote more business investment as existing
businesses take advantage of infill growth

So, I urge the Council to do the smart thing. Let’s not just accept more and more sprawl because it’s easy in the short term. Because in
the longer term for our children and beyond expanding needlessly is an environmental mistake and a lost opportunity to improve our
county’s current infrastructure. The current plan being considered really doesn’t solve our desire to make things better for everyone.

Look inward in Clark County to realize the potential for exiting new growth opportunities that will enhance the entire region, instead of
just extending and perpetuating all of our current problems.




Bob Johnson
bob@johnsonsf.com

Dear County Council

The WA Department of Commerce's evaluation of our county's draft Comprehensive Plan Update
and has pointed out the plan's flaws. Specifically that there was insufficient analysis to support
the expansion of urban growth areas outside of Vancouver and that it appeared that there is
sufficient land for projected population increases in Clark County. There is no legal justification to
expand the Urban Growth Areas.

In addition, there is no model or mechanism to determine what lands to even consider to de-
designate from prime agricultural lands and farmlands of statewide importance. These are lands
are a resource, irreplaceable, and necessary to keep our community sustainable, to provide
habitat for wildlife, and to help safeguard water and air quality. It seems in the current plan, land
adjacent to existing development is the primary factor in removing protected lands into the UGA,
even though that is the definition of sprawl.

I have lived in the city of Vancouver for 27 years and have witnessed the development of once
open farm and wooded lands in east Vancouver and north of Hazel Dell. There is a huge difference
between sprawl and thoughtful development. There is no legal justification to de-designate
agricultural lands.
The Commerce Department has given the county an opportunity to correct its choice of Comp
Plan alternatives, to avoid litigation, delays, loss of funding. It's like Commerce has given you the
answers to a high stakes exam. I urge you to consider and incorporate their responses into the
Comprehensive Plan and revert to the alternative with no urban growth area expansions.

Our county's Agricultural Commission had it right in unanimously voting to keep all agricultural
designations and asking for a moratorium on upzoing of lands that meet the legal criteria for ag
designation. I urge you to consider the people in the future who will have to live with our
decisions. Stop UGA expansions and to stop the de-designation of agricultural lands.

Thank you.

Chair Marshall and Councilors,

The Vancouver Bicycle Club (VBC) writes in strong support of the recommendations submitted
to you by the dark Communities Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee (BPAC) and to
ask the Council to consider additional commitments that would make those recommendations
stick.


VBC is one of the largest and longest-standing recreational and community cycling
organizations in Southwest Washington. VBC's mission is: "To enjoy and spread a passion
for safe cycling in Vancouver and dark County through group and event rides, giving,
and community service. " We have been a presence in the community for over 54 years.
Today we're about 600 riders strong, and last year our members rode over 136, 000miles .
together across more than 700 group rides. We have rides going out nearly,every,day ofthe
week, year-round, at paces and distances for every level of rider, many of which are open and
accessible to VBC members and.non-members alike.. We ride all over the Vanco.uver metro area
- the City ofVancouver, dark County, and elsewherethroughout,the .region. Every July.we,
host our signature event, the Ride Around Ciark County, with routes for every kind of rider from
an all-abilities explorer route up to a 100-miie century. We. are the'people who experience the
county's active transportation network exactly as rt is built: excellent in places, disconnected as
a whole, and unsafe in many predictable, well-known locations.

BPAC Chair Zilavy's letter identifies the right next steps; we want to emphasize what this all
looks like from our perspective, and what in our view must support these steps so real solutions
are successfully implemented. Our central point: the transportation element of the
Comprehensive Plan is a matter of safety, and we ask the Council to judge it on whether it
makes it possible for people to live, work, and move around within dark County without a car,
and without being killed or seriously injured on dangerous county roads.

When BPAC delivered its annual update to the Council on May 6, 2026, VBC members filled the
room. Three councilors spoke candidly about the state of the county's active transportation
network, asked BPAC for specific projects to push through the pipeline, and invited BPAC to
engage with the Council more than once a year. We. support the work BPAC is doing in this
regard, gnd we agreewith BPAC's emphasis p^the^Qundatic^al^i^                        at hand: not just which
projects, but howthe .county c.an reahsUcally, fund, :pMoritize-and ^ them-.. .. , .. . ;
                             . '. :" .'. 'i. ^ . ':.   ;'-!7. l^-;"'i.Cl ' :..... .^ ..
Our meetings with stakeholders, attendance at public and. private meetings, participation in
community events, and review of media, coverage and public records a!) reveal an undisputed


                                                                                                   Page 1 of 7
truth: there is an urgent and unmet need for human-scale infrastructure in this county, dark
County is growing, traffic volumes are growing with it, and the network for walking, hiking, and
rolling was not built for the population the county has today, let alone the population it is
planning for and will inevitably experience in the future. -That is not the failure-of any single
project, budget cycle, or Council. It is the accumulated result of decades of individual decisions
that in too many cases treated the driver as the only userworth designing for and everyone else
as an afterthought. Each of those decisions looked small at the time. Together they produced a
county where a trip to a school, a park, a store, or a bus stop is often unsafe or effectively
impossible for anyone not in a car. This also produced a situation that is.practically and
financially untenable. As City of VancouverManagerLon Pluckhahn explained to this council
last summer, "the urban growth area was either going to bankrupt the county or bankrupt the
city[. ]" KOIN 6 News, Aug1, 2025.

Problems built over decades are corrected over decades, which is exactly why the
transportation element of the County's Comprehensive Plan update matters. A comprehensive
plan is one of the few moments when a county can change its defaults. The choices made in
this transportation element will determine what gets built, and what quietly becomes impossible
to build, for a generation. We are asking the Council to treat that as the opportunity it is, so that
dark County remains a livable and pleasant place to be as it grows, and not simply a harder
and more dangerous place to get around.

Everything that follows is, at bottom, about safety. The gaps in the county's network are not
merely inconvenient. They are where people get hurt and a source of disconnection in our
communities. A missing sidewalk puts a pedestrian in a travel lane. A bike lane that ends at a
bridge or an intersection delivers a rider into merging traffic at the exact moment the road
becomes most dangerous. An unsignaled crossing on a five-lane arterial asks a child, or
someone using a walker, to judge gaps in 45-mph traffic. These are not accidents in the sense
of being unforeseeable. They are the predictable output of design decisions, which means they
can be anticipated, prioritized, and prevented.

We would add that safety does not depend on how many people walk, ride, or roll today. A
resident who never intends to walk, bike, or roll still has an interest in a county where a teenager
can get to school without a car, and where drivers themselves are not the last line of defense
against roads and other infrastructure designs that put pedestrians in harm's way.

PART I: We support BPAC's four recommendations

1. Fund the update to the 2010 Bicycle and Pedestrian Master Plan

We agreewith BPAC that this is the single most effective step available to the Council, and we
support the specific request: fund the update at the $200, 000-$300, 000 Jevel identified in
BPAC's tetter, consistent with the recommendation already carried in Table 12 of the
Transportation Capital Facilities Plan. The county is planning for 2045 while relying on an



                                                                  Vancouver Bicycle Club - Public Comment
                                                                                               Page 2 of 7
unfulfilled plan adopted in 2010, for a county that has since changed substantially in population,
land use, and travel patterns.

2. Update Title 40, including Section 40. 350. 015, so the code defines real facility options

We support BPAC's recommendation that the Title 40 revisions in this update address Section
40. 350. 015. As BPAC notes, the current code leans on in-road, six-foot bike lanes as a
near-universal answer. That standard is why our members regularly find themselves in a painted
stripe next to 45-mph traffic on roads where nobody would let their kid ride (which, in many
places, is no longer visible due to vehicle traffic erasing those painted stripes). A stripe of paint
is not a safety treatment; physical separation is, and the required degree of separation should
follow from vehicle speed and volume rather than from a single default dimension. Different
roadways and contexts require different treatments: protected bike lanes, buffered ianes,
shared-use paths, and other context-sensitive designs. For this reason, we support BPAC's
reference to the county's multimodal level-of-stress (MMLOS) standards, and we ask that those
standards be adopted and applied in project design and in development review.

3. Increase the pace of bicycle and pedestrian capital delivery

We share BPAC's assessment that moving one or two bicycle and pedestrian projects forward in
a given year cannot build a connected network or close the gaps that already exist. We support
revising the Public Works capital selection criteria accordingly. In revising them, we ask the
Council to take care not to trade away safety weight in exchange for throughput.

We also endorse BPAC's framing of the goal: a network that is safe and useful for the average
person, not just for experienced cyclists. That distinction matters to us as a club, because our
members are among the most confident riders in the county and even we route around large
parts of it.

4. Active transportation is the practical investment in a constrained budget.

BPAC is right that constrained 20-year revenue makes prioritization more important, not less.
Active transportation delivers meaningful transportation value at a fraction of the cost of major
roadway expansion, and safe sidewalks, protected bike facilities, and shared-use paths give
residents a real option for reaching parks, schools, businesses, and transit stops without a car.
The barriers that keep people from choosing those options today are largely the product of past
investment decisions, which means they are within the Council's power to change.

We would also observe that the present arrangement is not free. Serious injuries and fatalities
on county roads carry substantial public costs - emergency response, medical care, lost
productivity, and liability exposure - and none of those costs appear in a capital budget even
though the county and its residents pay them. Safety investment is not simply spending set
against a constrained budget. It reduces and offsets costs the county is already absorbing.



                                                                Vancouver Bicycle Club - Public Comment
                                                                                              Page 3 of 7
PART II: Additional things we ask the Council to consider

1. Adopt the Active Transportation Network as a commitment, not a map

The draft plan includes a proposed Active Transportation Network, developed to satisfy the
Growth Management Act requirement for an active transportation component. We generally
support an Active Transportation Network, and also understand that the particulars of this
network must be adaptablewith the passage of time. But a network drawn on a map and a
network the county is committed to building are two different things, and that difference is most
of what our comment, and BPAC's proposal, are about. We ask that the transportation element
adopt the Active Transportation Network as a policy commitment to a connected countywide
system, rather than as an inventory of individual projects.

Three things give that commitment meaning:

    .   Connectivity as a requirement, not an aspiration. An isolated sidewalk, or a bike lane
        that ends where the funding ended, has limited transportation value and creates a
        specific hazard at the point where it ends. The plan should direct that projects be
        prioritized for meaningful connections to a comprehensive active transportation network.
    .   Design for people of all ages and abilities. Safety should be the primary selection
        criterion, and facilities should be usable by a 7-year-old and a 70-year-old alike. This is
        the same standard BPAC asks for (e. g. MMLOS), and it is the difference between a
        network that changes travel behavior and one that serves the people already willing to
        ride in traffic.
    .   Prioritize underserved areas. The plan should identify where residents today have no
        safe walking or hiking connection at all. The county's own planning materials indicate
        that existing bicycle facilities are concentrated in the southwestern portion of the county,
        which makes countywide connectivity a matter of basic geographicfairness as well as
        sound network design.

This is consistent with BPAC's adopted work plan, which calls for completing a countywide
Active Transportation Network by closing existing gaps and providing meaningful connections to
each city network. We ask the Council to give that goal the force of adopted policy.

2. Name the size of the backlog and adopt a phased strategy to close it

The county's own planning work identifies roughly $490 million in active transportation needs
over the next 20 years, alongside approximately $537 million in large capital projects. Those
totals are drawn from the county draft Chapter 5 (Transportation) and the companion Capital
Facilities Plan chapter and appendices presented to the Council at the July 15, 2026 work
session. A plan that identifies a half-bitlion dollars of need without a structural funding or ,
prioritization change is not a plan; it is a record of a growing deficit.




                                                                  Vancouver Bicycle Club - Public Comment
                                                                                                Page 4 of 7
We ask the Council to direct that the transportation element describe a realistic, phased strategy
for closing the active transportation gap, including expected annual investment levels. We
further ask that the strategy identify how much of that need is safety-driven - crossings,
neighborhood greenways, separation on high-speed arterials, and sidewalk gaps on routes to
schools and transit stops - and that the safety-driven share be phased first. This gives BPAC's
"increase the pace" recommendation a clear target.

3. Make progress publicly trackable.

A plan the public cannot follow is a plan the public cannot help deliver. Most of what the Council
adopts in this element will be carried out over many years by staff and future Councils who were
not in the room when it was written, and today a resident has no straightforward way to tell
whether the active transportation commitments in an adopted county pian are actuaily moving.

Therefore, we ask the Council to direct that this transportation element be accompanied by
accountability any resident can check:

    .   A published list of the active transportation projects and policy commitments the plan
        adopts, each with an expected phase or timeframe.
    .   An annual public report, delivered to the Council and posted online, showingwhat was
        funded, what was built, what slipped, and why.
    .   A short set of outcome measures tracked consistently over time, beginning with the
        measures that matter most - pedestrian and cyclist incidents, serious injuries, and
        fatalities, along with where on the network they occur- alongside network miles
        completed, crossings added, and planned gaps closed;
    .   A standing place on the calendar for public input on that report, whether through BPAC,
        an annual update to the Council, or both.

None of this requires new technology or meaningful new staff cost. It is the mechanismthat lets
residents and organizations like ours engage constructively and consistently rather than leaving
us to second-guess. When we can see what is planned and where it stands, our comment and
our publictestimony can speak to the projects the county is actually trying to deliver. It also
protects the Council's own work, because a documented record of progress is what keeps a
20-year plan from quietly becoming a shelf document.

4. Stop losing ground in development review and capital projects.

Too often, roadwayand development projects are approved in ways that foreclose a future
walking or hiking connection, and the county then pays far more to retrofit it later, or never does.
The cost of that is not only financial. For as long as the connection is missing, people continue
to eitherwalk and ride there anyway in conditions nobody designedfor them, or to adapt their
lifestyles to a built environment that requires them to depend on a car for all trips. This is the
quiet counterpart to BPAC's Title 40 recommendation: better standards' only help if they are
required at all relevant times along the lifecycle of our city. We ask that the plan direct Public

                                                                Vancouver Bicycle Club - Public Comment
                                                                                              Page 5 of 7
Works and Community Development to evaluate arterial projects and developments for their
effect on the planned active transportation network, and to document those evaluations. All
relevant county standards should also require that new development help complete the planned
network, rather than add additional disconnected fragments to it.

Conclusion: what we are asking the Council to do

Adopt BPAC's recommendations:

   .   Fund the update to the Bicycle and Pedestrian Master Plan at the $200,000-$300,000
       level, on a defined timeline.
   .   Direct that the Title 40 revisions in this update address Section 40. 350. 015 and establish
       design guidance for the full range of active transportation facilities named in the draft
       plan.
   .   Revise Public Works capital selection criteria to increase the pace of bicycle and
       oedestrian project delivery.
   .   Adopt multimodal level-of-service and level-of-stress standards, and apply them in
       project design and development review, consistentwith the Arterial Atlas and RTC's
       regional plan.

And considerthe following:

   .   Adopt the Active Transportation Network as a policy commitment to a connected
       countywide system, with connectivity, all-ages-and-abiiities safety, and priority for
       underserved areas as explicit prioritization criteria.
   .   Adopt a Transportation Element that states the size of the active transportation backlog
       and describes a funded, phased strategy for closing it, with the safety-driven share of
       that backlog identified and phased first.
   .   Direct staff to publish an annual, public progress report on the active transportation
       commitments in this plan, covering spending, projects delivered, projects delayed, and a
       consistent set of outcome measures led by pedestrian and cyclist fatalities and serious
       injuries, with a regular opportunity for public input.
   .   Direct staff to evaluate and document the effect of arterial projects and significant
       developments on the planned active transportation network.

BPAC has advised you what the county should do, and our members' experience on these
roads points to the same conclusion. What matters now is whetherthis plan becomes a network
people can actually use - and, above all, one they can use safely.

Subject
Comprehensive Plan Final Adoption Hearing

Date of Hearing
Thu, 10/01/2026

Comment
Dear Chair Marshall, and Councilors Belkot, Fuentes, Little, and Yung,

I am a Vancouver Washington resident and I strongly suggest that you consider the following for
the comprehensive plan.

1) Align greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets with the City of Vancouver’s reduction
targets.
2) No expansion of UGBs or de-designation of agricultural resource lands.
3) Draft a supplemental EIS with appropriate up-zoning to accommodate housing and
employment targets.

There is a large coalition of various individuals and organizations that are also advocating for the
considerations including: Green Party of Southwest Washington, Southwest Washington Equity
Coalition, Southwest Washington LULAC, Vietnamese Community of Clark County, Hispanic
Disability Support SWWA (Pasitos Gigantes), Sierra Club Loowit Group, Western Institute for
Agriculture and Food Security Foundation, Pacific Islander Community Association of WA
(PICAWA), iUrban Teen, Vancouver Metro LULAC Council 47026, Columbia Riverkeeper,
Vancouver Audubon Society, SW WA Victory Food Project, Fourth Plain Forward, Alliance for
Community Engagement (ACE), and Cycle Vancouver.

I have provided details for each item below.

1) Align greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets with the City of Vancouver’s reduction
targets.

According to Community Planning staff, the currently proposed GHG emissions reduction targets
for unincorporated Clark County within the Comp Plan Update Climate Element Draft are
insufficient and create risk in meeting the statewide 2050 target established in RCW 70A.45.020.
Unincorporated Clark County and the City of Vancouver account for 84% of Clark County GHG
emissions, 40% and 44% respectively. Adopting the City of Vancouver’s targets of 80% reduction
in GHG emissions by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2040 would align with the responses of a
majority of the Clark County Climate Advisory Group and reflect the bold leadership and sense of
urgency necessary to address our rapidly accelerating climate emergency.

As noted by staff, a significant portion of Clark County GHG emissions are produced by sources
like transportation (36% of total emissions) and agriculture and tree loss (21%) which are out of
County control. We strongly agree that establishing more ambitious reduction targets could
create the necessary sense of urgency and innovation while allowing more time to adapt further if
the County falls short of interim goals. Additionally, by adopting reduction targets aligned with the
City of Vancouver, the County could model strong leadership on addressing climate change as
Washougal, Ridgefield, and Camas--which has a high 2022 GHG emissions baseline--align on
their own reduction targets in the near future. As a reminder, there is no penalty for missing more
ambitious targets. However, Clark County has the opportunity to work alongside the City of
Vancouver in reducing our carbon footprint and providing environmental and public health
benefits for the majority of residents sooner.

2) No expansion of UGBs or de-designation of agricultural resource lands.

Additionally, we would like to echo the sentiment of the majority of prior written public comment
and verbal testimony for the Preferred Alternative hearing in April, and FutureWise’s public
comment dated July 30, 2026, regarding the expansion of UGBs and de-designation of agricultural
resource lands protected by the Growth Management Act. Reducing urban sprawl by
accommodating projected housing and employment targets within existing urban growth areas
through appropriate up-zoning and development could help reduce vehicle miles traveled and
associated GHG emissions. Additionally, we strongly believe that in order to meet the goal of
“promot[ing] holistic and resilient food economies” to expand local food security as stated in the
Chapter 14 Climate Element draft, legally protected agricultural resource lands should not be de-
designated. As accelerating climate change increases surface air temperatures, the frequency of
extreme weather events, and threatens crop yields and the stability of the global food system, our
reliance on our local food system will become more important than ever. As it was stated in
public testimony at the Preferred Alternative Hearing, “we cannot eat concrete.”

We would also like to specifically highlight the Washington Department of Commerce’s recent
letter to the Council dated September 22nd, 2026, which reinforces our understanding that the
Vacant Buildable Lands Model indicates that the current UGBs are sufficient to accommodate
projected growth. Additionally, we agree with Commerce that the County has not clearly
identified “insufficient capacity for housing needs, document[ed] how they have evaluated zoning
changes to accommodate deficits in housing capacity, and then document[ed] sufficient
capacity with any UGA changes after these previous steps.” Regarding a Transfer of Development
Rights Program (Policy 1.1.24), Commerce is clear that “TDR programs are not intended to be
used as a mechanism to expand UGA Boundaries.” We also strongly believe that TDRs should not
be used to facilitate the de-designation and destruction of protected agricultural lands.
Additionally, TDRs should not be used to essentially leverage a loophole to designate and transfer
development rights of lands that should have already been designated and protected based on
the 2025 Clark County Agricultural Lands Study. Further, Commerce is clear that the de-
designation of agricultural resource lands has “historically has not been found to be defensible by
the Growth Management Hearings Board.”

3) Draft a supplemental EIS with appropriate up-zoning to accommodate housing and
employment targets.

We are again urging you to do the right thing and call for a supplemental EIS (WAC 197-11-405)
leveraging the Vacant Buildable Lands Model data to create a viable alternative with appropriate
up-zoning that omits or greatly reduces UGB expansion, ideally eliminating the de-designation of
valuable agricultural resource lands which are protected by the Growth Management Act and
critical to safeguarding our local food system.

To be clear, we are not anti-development. We are simply calling for appropriate and responsible
development, aligned with the intent of, and in compliance with, the Growth Management Act.
Clark County is a beautiful place blessed with abundant resources including prime soils for
farming. We are confident that our County leaders are capable of drafting an alternative and
Comp Plan Update that will accommodate the need for housing and employing new neighbors
while also protecting our resources and food security.

Thank you.
Allen C.

Submitted on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 3:15 PM

Name
Cynthia Hosszu
Phone Number
3606060691

Email Address
chosszu@hotmail.com

Subject
Comp Plan Hearing

Date of Hearing
Thu, 10/01/2026

Comment
I oppose approving additional high-density development, major land-use changes, or growth-
dependent projects in and around the NE 179th Street corridor until transportation infrastructure,
emergency access, utilities, drainage, and other public facilities are adequately funded and
available to serve that growth.
This is especially important near Ridgefield, where rural homes, working agricultural land,
livestock properties, and existing road users are already affected by congestion, incomplete road
connections, unsafe intersections, and identified transportation-concurrency deficiencies. The
County should not respond to those deficiencies by weakening, redefining, or obscuring what
qualifies as a failing road. The County should correct the actual infrastructure problem.
Washington’s Growth Management Act requires counties to prohibit development approval when
development would cause the level of service on a locally owned or operated transportation
facility to fall below the standards adopted in the comprehensive plan, unless needed
improvements or strategies are concurrent with development. “Concurrent” means
improvements are in place when development occurs or a financial commitment exists to
complete them within six years. RCW 36.70A.070(6)(b). State rules define adequate public
facilities as those with enough capacity to serve development without reducing service below
locally established minimums. WAC 365-196-210 and WAC 365-196-840.
Clark County Code 40.350.020 establishes the County’s Transportation Concurrency
Management System. County materials use a corridor volume-to-capacity standard of 0.90 or
less, meaning conditions above 90 percent of capacity are deficient. County materials have
identified failing conditions in the NE 179th Street area, including NE 179th Street between NE
29th and NE 50th avenues and the NE 179th Street/NE 50th Avenue intersection, identified as
Level of Service F.
The County’s own road projects confirm that substantial capacity problems exist. The NE 179th
Street corridor improvements are intended to accommodate traffic generated by development,
and the NE 179th Street/NE 29th Avenue project replaces an all-way stop intersection with a
roundabout at a listed budget of $23.2 million. These needs do not disappear because the County
changes a formula, raises a threshold, alters a calculation method, or relabels a deficiency.
Changing the definition of failure does not build missing roads, relieve backed-up intersections,
reduce cut-through traffic, improve emergency response, or make roads safer for school buses,
pedestrians, cyclists, farm equipment, hay trucks, livestock trailers, delivery vehicles, and
commuters. Residents do not experience traffic through a spreadsheet. They experience it while
sitting in congestion, trying to leave driveways, using rural roads, moving agricultural equipment,
and depending on emergency services.
If roads are failing under the standard that applied when development was approved or proposed,
the County should fund and complete needed improvements, require enforceable developer
mitigation, phase or delay growth, or deny proposals that cannot meet concurrency. It should not
redefine the problem out of existence.
The NE 179th Street area includes productive agricultural land, livestock acreage, rural
residences, and working farms. Agricultural land is not unused land waiting for urban-scale
development. It supports local food production, farm and livestock businesses, rural jobs,
suppliers, and the character of the area. Once land is paved over, fragmented, isolated from
access, or made impractical to operate, the loss is largely permanent.
Transportation projects and development must preserve practical access for tractors, farm
trucks, livestock trailers, hay deliveries, equipment, and rural driveways. The County must
evaluate the effects of road widening, increased traffic, drainage changes, utility corridors,
lighting, noise, and parcel fragmentation on working farms.
High-density housing immediately adjacent to livestock acreage will create foreseeable conflicts
for newcomers and existing residents. Farms and livestock operations involve normal, lawful
activities and conditions: animal sounds, odors, manure management, dust, flies, fencing,
equipment, trailers, deliveries, and seasonal or early-morning work. Residents who move next to
these operations may object to the very activities that make farming possible. Meanwhile,
established farmers and livestock owners may face complaints, trespass, loose dogs, litter,
traffic hazards, liability concerns, and pressure to curtail lawful use of their property.
The County should not create these conflicts by placing incompatible density beside existing
farms and livestock properties. Any development proposed near working agricultural land should
include meaningful buffers, clear agricultural disclosure notices, protections against trespass
and unleashed dogs, safe agricultural access, and enforceable protection of existing lawful farm
practices..
I ask the Council to retain a clear, objective, and protective transportation-concurrency standard
under Clark County Code 40.350.020. Do not change the standard merely to make failing roads
appear compliant. Publish current traffic data, volume-to-capacity calculations, intersection
level-of-service data, funding sources, construction schedules, and remaining deficiencies for
the NE 179th Street corridor. Require secure, enforceable funding and completion schedules
before treating improvements as concurrent with development. Delay, condition, or deny
development that would cause or worsen a concurrency failure. Require developers to pay a fair
and enforceable share of the road, intersection, drainage, utility, and safety improvements their
projects require.
Clark County should build and fund infrastructure first, protect working land and established
residents, and then allow development at a pace the transportation system can actually support.
Approving additional growth while roads already fail—and then changing the definition of failure
to avoid accountability—would shift costs and risk to existing residents, farmers, businesses, and
taxpayers.

Name
Alexander Gerchikov

Phone Number
3606093366

Email Address
gerchikov.alex@gmail.com

Subject
Housing Stability for 55+ Manufactured Homes

Date of Hearing
Thu, 10/01/2026

Comment

I am writing to share critical information regarding housing stability and health risks for residents
at Cascade Park Estates, a 55+ manufactured home park in Clark County.

This community provides essential affordable housing for older adults who own their homes but
rent the underlying land. However, rising rents, potential park sales, and the upcoming expiration
of the Clark County Redevelopment moratorium in February 2027 create significant instability for
these seniors, who live on fixed incomes.

Medical research highlights the severe health impacts of housing instability:

- "The hazard ratio for death among older adults experiencing housing insecurity ranges from 1.5
to 1.75, representing a 50% to 75% higher risk of mortality compared to housed peers" (JAMA,
2026).
- If homelessness occurs, mortality risk more than doubles, potentially reducing expected life
expectancy by 10 to 20 years. These outcomes are driven by stress-related worsening of heart
disease, diabetes, respiratory illness, depression, and cognitive decline.

Manufactured home park residents are uniquely vulnerable for several reasons:

- Many homes cannot be moved due to age or structural limitations.
- Relocation assistance rarely covers actual moving costs.
- Fixed incomes severely limit access to alternative housing.
- Pre-existing medical conditions make relocation or displacement life-threatening.

Heare is PUBLIC-HEALTH IMPACT CHART

Housing Situation Change in Mortality Health Impact Description
Risk
Stable Housing Baseline Chronic conditions manageable; lower stress.

Housing insecurity +50%-75% Worsening heart disease,diabetes,COPD, cognition

Forced Relocation / +75%-100% Acute crises; hospitalizations; loss of continuity of care
eviction

Homelessness >2x (100%+ Severe decline; high mortality; loss of 19-20 years of
life.




While Clark County's proposed Manufactured Home Park (MHP) Overlay Zone would reduce
redevelopment pressure, it does not regulate rent or prevent park sales. Without stronger
protections, these older adults face conditions associated with a dramatically increased
mortality risk.

Preserving 55+ manufactured home parks is both a vital housing strategy and a critical public
health intervention. [Insert call to action or concluding sentence, e.g., "I welcome the opportunity
to discuss potential policy solutions to protect these residents."]

                  Transportation Concurrency Analysis
                Heartwood North Subdivision — PLD-2025-00114
              Public Hearing: June 11, 2026 — Hearing Examiner Daniel Kearns

I. Summary
Heartwood North should be denied. Clark County’s concurrency regulations, CCC 40.350.020,
were written to stop development from being approved onto roads that can no longer carry it.
Rather than apply that code as written, staff have built a mechanism that keeps approving
development on corridors that already fail. The reasons for denial include:

   •   Three concurrency corridor segments exceed the mandatory 0.90 V/C standard in
       (G)(1)(a) at 2029 buildout — NE 119th Street (eastbound 1.10) and NE 99th Street
       (eastbound 0.99, westbound 0.97).

   ●   The study omitted regionally significant corridors within the required two-mile radius that
       Exhibit A documents as failing — SR 503 (V/C 0.928–1.066, evaluated only at its
       intersections), NE 152nd Avenue (0.93), and NE 76th Street (1.034–1.06) — none
       evaluated as concurrency corridors, as (D) and (G)(1)(a) require.
   ●   Two unsignalized intersections fail their applicable (G)(1)(c) standard — signal warrants
       are met, so the standard is LOS D, and both report LOS E or F.
   ●   The compliance finding rests on two devices found nowhere in the code — an
       intersection-LOS substitution and an (F)(9)/HCM capacity adjustment — neither of which
       can move the (G)(1)(a) capacity threshold.
   ●   No County improvement in place or financially committed within six years under (F)(6)
       brings any failing segment below 0.90, so (E)(3) requires denial.

Many of these same issues arose in the 174th Street Subdivision hearing; relevant documents
from that proceeding are attached as further explanation of the issues here.

What the Traffic Study Evaluated

intersections between them as indicated in the Heartwood North Subdivision Transportation
Impact Analysis (Kittelson & Associates, Inc., February 12, 2026) (the “TIA”). This is the
situation residents face every day: full roads, and long waits at the intersections.

The Two-Mile Study Area the Code Required
The corridors and intersections a concurrency study must evaluate are set by code, not by
selection. Under (D), the study area is sized by the development’s peak-period trips — two
miles for 51 to 250 units— and within that radius the study must analyze all affected corridors
and intersections of regional significance and account for trips on all collector and arterial
roadways; (G)(1)(a) requires that corridor measurements also be made for state highways of
regional significance. The study does not apply what the code requires — it set scope “based on
a review of existing travel patterns and consistency with the scope of analysis prepared for the
approved Heartwood Subdivision to the south,” with intersections “identified in collaboration with
Clark County staff” — a discretionary selection, not the trip-based radius the code requires.

The sixteen studied intersections trace a narrow band along NE 99th and NE 119th Streets, not
a two-mile radius. Figure 2 plots an estimated two-mile radius centered on the site as the study
locates it — south of NE 119th Street between NE 137th and NE 143rd Avenues — against
those intersections. The studied band falls well inside the required circle in every direction and
is shallowest to the north. The boundaries shown are approximated.



                                                                                                              2
   Figure 2. Estimated two-mile concurrency radius under CCC 40.350.020(D), against the sixteen studied
                                               intersections.

The gap is not theoretical. Exhibit A — the Failing Corridor Evaluation Memorandum (PLS
Engineering, Daniel Stumpf, PE) — reports regionally significant corridors operating above 0.90
within roughly two miles of the site that the study did not evaluate as corridors — among them
SR 503 (the state highway the development’s trips feed, scored only at its intersections), NE
152nd Avenue, and NE 76th Street. A study drawn to the required radius would have had to
account for them.

approach. The east end, NE 124th Avenue / NE 99th Street, is the one genuinely acceptable
intersection of the four — overall LOS B (16.6 seconds), approaches A through C.

III. The Unsignalized Intersections Do Not Meet Their Applicable Standard
Under (G)(1)(c), an unsignalized intersection of regional significance must achieve LOS E or
better if warrants are not met, and LOS D or better if warrants are met. Where a warrant is met,
LOS E is already a failure.

NE 124th Ave / NE 119th St, a two-way stop with NE 119th uncontrolled. The study reports
LOS E in both peaks and states that “signal warrants are met.” With warrants met, the


                                                                                                   5
applicable standard is D, so LOS E does not meet it. The intersection draws a concurrency pass
only through the separate (G)(1)(c)(1) mitigation trigger — the development adds fewer than five
peak-hour trips to the failing northbound approach — which excuses the developer from
mitigating but does not make the intersection compliant.

NE 132nd Ave / NE 119th St, a two-way stop with NE 119th uncontrolled. The northbound
approach is LOS F in both peaks; Signal Warrant 2 (four-hour) is met. The applicant
volunteered a northbound left-turn lane, but the study’s own Table 8 shows the mitigated
approach remains LOS F in both AM and PM (PM delay improves only from 82.7 to 73.4
seconds). The study frames the mitigation as restoring the approach to “better than pre-
development background conditions” — offsetting the development’s increment, not achieving
the standard.

IV. The Concurrency Standard the Code Requires
Study scope — (D)(2)(b), (D)(4), (D)(5). The study must account for trips assigned to all
collector and arterial roadways and analyze all affected corridors and intersections of regional
significance within the applicable radius. The radius is set by the development’s peak-period
trips: one mile for 50 or fewer, two miles for 51–250, and three miles for 251 or more. An
intersection of regional significance is one with at least three collector or arterial legs.

Approval gate — (E)(1) and (E)(3). No development may be approved until the Public Works
Director issues a concurrency approval (E)(1). The Director issues that approval only where the
development’s impacts do not cause the operating levels for the transportation corridors,
signalized intersections, and unsignalized intersections to fall below the (G) standards (E)(3). All
three categories are stated conjunctively.

Volunteered-mitigation path — (E)(5). The Director may approve and condition mitigation, if
volunteered, where it offsets the development’s impact “such that the operating levels will not
further deteriorate” — or where meeting the standard would cause significant SEPA impacts.
This is the only alternative to (E)(3).

Volume inputs — (F), including (F)(9). Section (F) governs the volume side of the ratio; (F)(9)
lets the Director consider “any other factors” affecting operating levels. It is a volume input and
cannot move the (G) capacity threshold.

Improvement credit — (F)(6). Only County improvements in place or financially committed
within six years count toward capacity.

Corridor standard — (G)(1)(a). The V/C ratio for each roadway segment shall not exceed 0.90
in each direction. Measurements shall be made for all collector and arterial segments in the
Vancouver UGA outside the City, and also for state highways of regional significance. Capacity
comes from the figures adopted in Table 40.350.020-1.

Interpretation through the manual — (G)(2). The LOS standards are “applied and interpreted
as stated in the administrative manual” ((G)(2)).




                                                                                                   6
Code controls over the manual — (N)(5). The administrative manual “shall be consistent with
and implement the provisions of this section,” and “to the extent the provisions of the manual
are inconsistent with the provisions of this section, the provisions of this section shall control”
((N)(5)).

V. The Recommended Approval Rests on Two Override Devices the Code
Does Not Authorize
The compliance finding rests on two distinct devices. The first is the intersection-mobility
override: the staff report concludes that the reported V/C over the NE 119th and NE 99th
corridors “does not represent roadway deficiencies, rather corridor mobility facilitated with good
intersection LOS,” and that no additional analysis or mitigation is required. The second is a
capacity-adjustment rationale built on the (F)(9) “real-world influences,” set out in the report’s
“Concurrency Corridors” section and addressed in Section VI. Both devices are deployed only
where a segment already exceeds 0.90 — in response to a failure, never as part of routine
analysis.

Neither device is found in the code. The corridor standard in (G)(1)(a) is a volume-to-capacity
limit; nothing in (G) authorizes substituting intersection performance for it, and nothing in (F),
including (F)(9), moves the (G) capacity threshold. The capacities are fixed by the code:
(G)(1)(a) draws them from the figures adopted in Table 40.350.020-1, and the “real-world
influences” the report invokes are not inputs the code permits to be substituted for those figures.
The (F)(9) capacity-adjustment rationale is also recent in writing — it appears in the Heartwood
concurrency report dated May 21, 2026 in the same multi-paragraph form as the reissued 174th
Street concurrency report of the identical date (Exhibit C) and the Traffic Engineering Section
Manager’s letter of the same date (Exhibit D), the day the 174th report was reissued, after the
April 23 hearing at which the override’s absence from the code was raised. The original 174th
Street concurrency report, which denied that subdivision (Exhibit B), did not contain this
rationale; it was added when the report was reissued as an approval (Exhibit C) on the last day
of the open record. Both are attached, and the difference between them is the added (F)(9) and
Highway Capacity Manual capacity language and the Director attribution, rather than a change
in the underlying corridor analysis.

The override sentence itself is not site-specific. The identical operative language appears in
unrelated County concurrency reports across the Salmon Creek / Fairgrounds and SR 503
areas — the reissued 174th Street report, Three Creeks East, and Four Creeks North among
them — reproduced by different developer-commissioned engineers before different examiners.
That repetition is the mark of a standardized device, not site-specific engineering judgment. In
the 174th proceeding, Hearing Examiner Turner observed from the bench that the controlling
provision, (G)(1)(a), “doesn’t say anything about level of service at either end” of a corridor; the
applicant’s attorney there acknowledged the override is not literally in the code; and several
development-side parties have asked the County Council to change the code rather than defend
it as written. (Exhibit E)




                                                                                                     7
VI. The Report Embeds the (F)(9) Theory as Standing Policy
The Heartwood report adds a “Concurrency Corridors” section that invokes (F)(9) and a five-
factor Highway Capacity Manual list — lane width, shoulders, heavy vehicles, grades, and
intersection spacing — to conclude that acceptable intersection LOS “allow[s]” an affirmative
finding of compliance with CCC 40.350.020(G)(1)(a) for a corridor that exceeds 0.90. The same
language, including the same five-factor list, is reproduced nearly verbatim from the Traffic
Engineering Section Manager’s letter in the 174th Street record (Exhibit D) — fixed policy text in
an unrelated project’s report, not site-specific analysis. But the Highway Capacity Manual does
not set the capacities for this test; (G)(1)(a) takes them from Table 40.350.020-1, where an
HCM field capacity has no place. The County advanced these as two separate threads in the
174th Street record: the volume-to-capacity override in the Traffic Engineering Section
Manager’s letter (Exhibit D), and the capacity-side argument — that real-world conditions justify
departing from the figures adopted in Table 40.350.020-1 — in the Transportation Division
Manager’s letter (Exhibit F). Responses to both are attached: to the v/c override (Exhibit G) and
to the capacity methodology (Exhibit H).

VII. CCC 40.350.020(F)(9) Does Not Authorize the Override
Section (F) governs the volume side of the ratio; (G) sets the capacity and the 0.90 line. A factor
under (F)(9) operates before the ratio is computed and cannot convert a completed (G)(1)(a)
exceedance into compliance. Had the HCM factors actually been applied, they would have
adjusted the capacity inputs and produced a recalculated V/C to test against 0.90 — but the
report performs no such calculation and presents no recalculated V/C; the factors are cited, not
applied. What the report substitutes instead is acceptable intersection performance, prompted
by the very fact that a segment exceeded 0.90. Using (F)(9) and an intersection-focused
“additional analysis” to call a corridor compliant at 0.90 while it stands at 1.10 leaves (E)(3) with
no corridor standard to enforce.

Even read as administrative interpretation, the override fails. The LOS standards are “applied
and interpreted as stated in the administrative manual” ((G)(2)), but (N)(5) caps that authority:
the manual “shall be consistent with and implement the provisions of this section,” and where
inconsistent “the provisions of this section shall control.” An interpretation that sets aside the
0.90 corridor standard is inconsistent with the section, and the section governs. Counsel for one
of the party’s of record noted this concern in the 174th Street Subdivision hearing as well (Exhibit
I)

VIII. The Corridor V/C Standard Is Binding, Not Discretionary
The staff report treats the 0.90 ratio as advisory — “a key engineering indicator” — and finds a
segment compliant on acceptable intersection performance even where the ratio exceeds 0.90.
The standard is not advisory. The Comprehensive Plan’s transportation element (Exhibit K)
adopts the corridor level-of-service standard “in terms of volume to capacity ratio for each
segment during the peak period” (Transportation Element, p. 140) and looks to CCC 40.350.020
for the figure; the GMA requires the County to enforce that adopted standard (RCW




                                                                                                   8
36.70A.070(6)(b)). Treating the ratio as a non-binding indicator leaves the ordinance failing to
implement the standard the plan adopts.

The plan keeps the corridor and intersection standards separate, as the code does — a corridor
segment V/C, a separate signalized-intersection standard, and a separate unsignalized
standard — and confers discretion only over whether to signalize an unsignalized intersection,
the plan’s counterpart to (G)(1)(c) (Transportation Element, p. 140). Nothing in the element lets
acceptable intersection LOS stand in for a failing corridor, and the plan defines a “deficient”
roadway as one that exceeds the adopted LOS standard (id.). A segment over 0.90 is, by the
plan’s own definition, a deficiency.

Countywide Planning Policy 5.0.5 commits the County to consistent, adopted level-of-service
standards and methodologies (Transportation Element, p. 151) — the opposite of a compliance
result set road-by-road at staff’s discretion. The legislative record is consistent: the Legislative
Intent Analysis (Exhibit J) shows the 2014 adoption describing intersection LOS as an
additional, protective floor, not a substitute for the corridor result, and the record contains no
Council action adopting an intersection-LOS override. Where an implementing ordinance is read
to conflict with the plan, the plan controls (Land Use Element, p. 25); only the reading that
enforces the corridor standard is consistent with the plan and the GMA.

IX. CCC 40.350.020(E)(3) Requires Denial of the Corridor Failures
The approval architecture is straightforward. Under (C) the review authority may approve,
condition, or deny; under (E)(1) it may not approve until a concurrency approval issues; and
under (E)(3) the Director issues that approval only where the operating levels for corridors,
signalized intersections, and unsignalized intersections do not fall below the (G) standards.
Three corridor segments fall below (G)(1)(a). (E)(3) is therefore not satisfied.

The override has no textual home. The only discretion for falling short of a standard is in
(G)(1)(c), confined to unsignalized intersections — and it speaks to whether the County must
build control there, not to corridors. The corridor standard in (G)(1)(a) carries no discretion
clause, no de-minimis threshold, and no causation carve-out; the intersection-level discretion
cannot be borrowed to excuse a corridor V/C failure.

The chain is therefore complete: the corridor segments fail (G)(1)(a); (E)(3) is not met; and
nothing in (G) authorizes an override. A concurrency approval cannot issue for these corridors,
and under (E)(1) and (C) the development must be denied.

X. No Funded Improvements Resolve the Corridor Failures Within Six Years
The study recommends “a more detailed operational analysis” before any major investment
decision and observes that NE 99th “appears to be constructed to its planned ultimate 3-lane
configuration” so that “it is unclear what, if any, additional capacity can be provided.” A
subdivision approval is such a decision, and the analysis the study calls for was not performed.
Under (F)(6), only a County improvement in place or financially committed within six years
creates capacity; the record establishes none that brings any failing segment below 0.90.




                                                                                                   9
XI. The Legislative Track Is the Place to Change the Standard
The County Council is considering a change to the concurrency standard pending the outcome
of the 174th Street Subdivision and this hearing. In the June 10th meeting, a work session was
requested to review LOS Standards. That effort originates in the dialogue at the 174th Street
Subdivision hearing, where the override’s absence from the code was raised. That a legislative
change is being pursued at all confirms the override is not in the code today. The standard
governing this application on June 11 is the code as adopted, and the Hearing Examiner should
apply (G)(1)(a) and (E)(3) as written. The timeline of events is outlined in Exhibit L.

XII. Conclusion and Request
Three Heartwood North corridor segments exceed the mandatory 0.90 V/C standard in the 2029
buildout year, and the analysis is incomplete because SR 503 was not evaluated as a corridor
though the code requires it and it is documented as failing. The compliance finding rests on an
intersection-LOS override that the code does not authorize and that does not hold up at the
approach level, and (E)(3) does not permit approval where the corridor standard is not met. On
this record the concurrency determination should not be sustained. The application should be
denied for failure to meet the corridor concurrency standard, or at a minimum remanded for a
concurrency analysis that applies the 0.90 corridor standard, evaluates all affected corridors and
intersections of regional significance within the applicable radius — including SR 503 — and
performs, rather than cites, any HCM capacity adjustment relied upon.

SCOPE OF THE REPORT
This analysis identifies the transportation-related impacts associated with the proposed development
and was prepared in accordance with Clark County’s transportation impact analysis requirements. The
study scope and overall study area for this project were determined based on a review of existing travel
patterns and consistency with the scope of analysis prepared for the approved Heartwood Subdivision
to the south. As required under Clark County Code 40.350.020, Transportation Concurrency
Management, the analysis was prepared to address the following transportation issues:

                Existing land use and transportation system conditions within the site vicinity during the
                 weekday AM and PM peak hours.
                Planned developments and transportation improvements in the study area.
                Future year 2029 background traffic conditions (without site development) during the
                 weekday AM and PM peak hours.
                Trip distribution estimates for the proposed development, including assignment of weekday
                 AM and PM peak hour trips to key concurrency corridor intersections.
                Future year 2029 total traffic conditions (with full buildout and occupancy of the proposed
                 development) during the weekday AM and PM peak hours.
                Volume-to-capacity ratios for applicable concurrency segments.

ANALYSIS METHODOLOGY

Performance Measures
Per Clark County standards, the level-of-service (LOS) performance measure was used to evaluate traffic
operations at the study intersections. The volume-to-capacity (v/c) ratio was used to evaluate roadway
segments for the concurrency analyses.

All operations analyses described in this report were performed in accordance with the procedures stated
in the 7th Edition Highway Capacity Manual (HCM 7th Edition – Reference 1) using Synchro 12 software.
There are exceptions at three intersections:
          The NE 114th Street and NE 132nd Avenue intersection (Study Intersection #6) was analyzed using
           2000 Highway Capacity Manual (HCM 2000 – Reference 2) as Synchro does not support the lane
           configurations of this stop-controlled intersection under HCM 7th Edition.
          The NE 119th Street and NE 152nd Avenue (Study Intersection #5) and NE 99th Street and NE 107th
           Avenue (Study Intersection #9) roundabouts were analyzed using the Sidra Standard Roundabout
           Capacity Model in SIDRA 9.1 software in accordance with the Washington State Department of
           Transportation (WSDOT) Sidra Policy Settings (Reference 3).

All intersection level-of-service analyses used a peak 15-minute flow rate during the weekday AM and
PM peak hours.


Facility Performance Standards


Clark County Operating Standards
Clark County Code (CCC) Section 40.350.020.G defines the County’s LOS standards for roadway segments
as well as signalized and unsignalized intersections.

     Roadway Segments
     Per CCC Section 40.350.020.G.1.a: “The maximum volume to capacity ratio for each roadway segment
     shall not exceed nine-tenths (0.9), when measured independently for each direction of travel.”

     Signalized Intersections
     Per CCC Section 40.350.020.G.1.b: “Individual movements at each signalized intersection of regional
     significance in the unincorporated county shall not exceed an average of two (2) cycle lengths or two
     hundred forty (240) seconds of delay (whichever is less).”




Kittelson & Associates, Inc.                                                                  Portland, Oregon
Heartwood North TIA                                                                                 Project #: 31137
February 2026                                                                                                Page: 6


       Unsignalized Intersections
       Per CCC Section 40.350.020.G.1.c: “All unsignalized intersections of regional significance in the
       unincorporated county shall achieve LOS E standards or better (if warrants are not met). If warrants
       are met, unsignalized intersections of regional significance shall achieve LOS D standards or better.
       Intersection control or mitigation of unsignalized intersections shall be at the discretion of the Public
       Works Director and shall not obligate the County to meet this LOS standard. However, proposed
       developments shall not be required to mitigate their impacts in order to obtain a concurrency
       approval unless:

                  (1)          The proposed development adds at least five (5) peak hour trips to a failing
                               intersection approach; and
                  (2)          The worst movement on the failing approach is worsened by the proposed
                               development. In determining whether the movement is worsened, the Public Works
                               Director shall consider trip volume, delay, and any other relevant factors.”


WSDOT Operating Standards
The study intersections along SR 503 (NE 117 th Avenue) are operated and maintained by WSDOT;
however, WSDOT does not designate SR 503 as being a highway of statewide significance 1. Accordingly,
County performance requirements apply at the study intersections along SR 503.

The existing conditions analysis identifies the site conditions and the current operational and geometric
characteristics of roadways within the study area. These conditions will be compared with future
conditions later in this report. Kittelson & Associates, Inc. (KAI) staff visited and inventoried the proposed
development site and surrounding area in June 2024 to observe site conditions, adjacent land uses,
existing traffic operations, and transportation facilities in the study area.


Site Conditions and Adjacent Land Uses
The study site is currently undeveloped. The majority of nearby land uses are residential, with commercial
uses to the west along NE 117th Avenue.

Transit Facilities
C-TRAN provides transit services within Clark County. Per C-Tran’s online schedule, (Reference 6) bus
service is provided by C-Tran Route 7 (Battle Ground) along NE 117th Avenue and C-Tran loop Route 72
(Orchards), along NE 99th Street. Additionally, Route 47 operates along NE 117 th Avenue, yet, with limited
services. The route offers only one trip during the AM peak, one at midday, and one during the PM peak
period.

Route 7 connects the Van Mall Transit Center to Southeast Grace Avenue and Southeast Rasmussen
Boulevard in Battle Ground and operates on weekdays from approximately 5:45 AM to 10:00 PM, with
30-minute headways for most of the day. On weekends, the route operates from approximately 6:45 AM
to 9:30 PM, with 60-minute headways throughout the day. The bus stop closest to the site is located on
NE 117th Avenue, approximately 800 feet south of NE 119 th Street.

Route 72 connects the Van Mall Transit Center to NE 117th Avenue and NE 99th Street and operates on
weekdays from approximately 5:00 AM to 9:00 PM, with 30-minute headways for most of the day. On
weekends, the route operates from approximately 7:15 AM to 8:00 PM, with 60-minute headways
throughout the day. The bus stop closest to the site is located at the southwest corner of NE 144 th Avenue
on NE 99th Street.

Traffic Volumes and Peak Hour Operations
Traffic counts were collected on a mid-week day in December 2025 while local schools were in session
during the morning (7:00 - 9:00 AM) and evening (4:00 - 6:00 PM) peak periods at the remaining study
intersections.

The heavy vehicle percentages in the traffic counts, shown in Appendix “A,” included Federal Highway
Administration Class 4 (buses) and Class 5 (two-axle, six-tire, single-unit vehicles) as heavy vehicles. Video
analysis indicates that the Class 4 and Class 5 vehicle types exceed the number of large freight vehicles
(such as Class 9 five-axle semitrailers) during the weekday PM peak period. Additional studies in the area
by others show lower heavy vehicle percentages, likely counting only these larger freight vehicles. Our
own analysis suggests that up to half of the heavy vehicles in these traffic counts are Class 4 and Class 5
vehicles. Therefore, the heavy vehicle percentage has been reduced by half across all intersections for
the existing, background, and total traffic PM peak hour (except where reducing the percentage would
split one heavy vehicle trip in half).


Existing Intersection Operations
Figures 4 and 5 summarize the traffic volumes and analysis results for the study intersections under
existing weekday AM and PM peak hour traffic conditions, respectively. As shown in the figures, the study
intersections currently operate acceptably per the County’s adopted standards as specified in CCC
Section 40.350.020.G. Appendix “B” includes the existing conditions level-of-service worksheets.

Concurrency Corridor V/C Ratios
Existing traffic volumes were compared with adopted Clark County capacity thresholds for corridor
segments to assess compliance with concurrency requirements. Table 3 summarizes the existing bi-
direction traffic volumes along the study area roadways during the weekday PM peak hour and reports
the V/C ratio along with the single direction roadway capacity as specified under Clark County Code
40.350.020 Transportation Concurrency Management and Table 40.350.020-1. As shown in Table 3, all
corridor segments operate below the County’s 0.90 V/C standard under existing conditions.

greater, the lane capacity shall be eight hundred (800) vehicles per hour. For roadways with lane widths between eleven (11) and twelve (12) feet

 intersection exhibited a crash rate exceeding the 1.0 crashes per MEV threshold. Appendix “C” includes

 NE 99th Street/NE 117th Street (SR 503)
 In addition to being the location of two reported fatal crashes, the NE 99 th Street/NE 117th Avenue
 intersection experienced a crash rate greater than 1.0 crashes per million entering vehicles (i.e., the
 metric used by the County to assess whether further analyses are warranted).


 Kittelson & Associates, Inc.                                                                                                                 Portland, Oregon
Heartwood North TIA                                                                              Project #: 31137
February 2026                                                                                            Page: 15


Of the 75 reported crashes at the intersection:
                18 involved rear-end crashes along the northbound and southbound NE 117 th Avenue
                 approaches.
                17 involved northbound left-turns and southbound through movements. Of these, 8
                 occurred between 3:00 and 6:00 PM with another 5 in the subsequent 6:00-7:00 PM hour.
                13 involved southbound left-turns and northbound through movements. Of these, 7
                 occurred between 3:00 and 6:00 PM.

There were two fatal crashes at this intersection. The first fatal crash happened in November 2022 when
a southbound pick-up turning left collided with a northbound pick-up, resulting in a death after
hospitalization. The second occurred in July 2024, involving a motorcycle overtaking at high speed and a
car making a left turn; both drivers made unsafe maneuvers, leading to a fatality at the hospital.

There were two pedestrian crashes reported at this intersection. The first crash involved a pedestrian
struck by a westbound left-turning vehicle. Per the crash records, the pedestrian ignored the traffic signal.
The second incident concerned a pedestrian being hit by a vehicle turning right, which did not yield the
right of way to the pedestrian during the turn.

The NE 99th Street/NE 117th Avenue Street intersection was reconstructed around 2017 at which time
the eastbound and westbound approaches were expanded from one travel lane to provide separate left-
turn, through, and right-turn lanes and a separate southbound right-turn lane was constructed. In
addition, bicycle lanes were added to NE 99th Street west of NE 117th Avenue and protected/permissive
left-turn signal control was provided on all approaches. It appears the intersection has operated with
protected/permissive on all approaches throughout the five-year crash data review period.

As noted above, approximately 41 percent of the reported crashes at the intersection involved
northbound and southbound left-turn movements. WSDOT changed the traffic signal phasing in February
2025 to operate protected only southbound left-turn phasing from 6:00 AM until 7:00 PM. Additionally,
northbound left-turn phasing is protected only from 9:00 AM until 7:00 PM. Outside of the given time
frames, the signals continue to run protected-permissive left turns.

Given the change in left-turn traffic control occurred after the crash reporting period, no crash trends
requiring mitigation were identified at this intersection through the crash data review.

TRANSPORTATION IMPACT ANALYSIS
The transportation impact analysis identifies how the study area’s transportation system will operate in
the year 2029, which corresponds to the three-year concurrency modeling period.


Year 2029 Background Traffic Conditions
The year 2029 background traffic conditions analysis identifies how the study intersections are projected
to operate prior to construction of the proposed Heartwood North development. This analysis includes
traffic attributed to planned developments and growth within the study area but does not include traffic
from the proposed development.


Planned Transportation Improvements
The 2026-2031 Clark County Transportation Improvement Program (Reference 7) includes Project
#301022 (NE 152nd Avenue – Padden Parkway to NE 99th Street). The County project includes the
installation of a traffic signal and the addition of northbound and southbound left-turn lanes at the
intersection of NE 152nd Avenue and NE 99th Street (Study Intersection #16). The project is funded and
scheduled for completion in 2027. As such, the new traffic signal can be assumed to be completed under
Year 2029 background traffic conditions for transportation concurrency purposes.


Regional Growth
The year 2029 background analysis reflects a two percent annual growth rate applied to existing traffic
volumes to account for general regional growth.


Planned Developments
Kittelson reviewed the in-process developments provided by Clark County staff and identified/included
in-process trips that impact the study intersections. Table 5 summarizes the planned developments and
provides an assessment of the expected trip generation associated with each development and the status
of each development in terms of percent complete or occupied. Figures illustrating the total projected
AM and PM peak hour in-process traffic volumes are provided in Appendix “D”.

Traffic Operations
Figures 6 and 7 summarize the traffic volumes and analysis results for the study intersections under year
2029 background traffic conditions during weekday AM and PM peak hours, respectively. Signal timing
was optimized at NE 99th Street/NE 117th Avenue to reflect the addition of in-process traffic. Appendix
“E” contains the year 2029 background traffic conditions worksheets.

As shown in the figures, all but two study intersections are projected to operate acceptably per the
County’s adopted standards as specified in CCC Section 40.350.020.G. The NE 117 th Avenue/NE 119th
Street intersection is projected to operate at an overall LOS F during the PM peak hour; however, all
individual movements satisfy the County’s delay performance standard of an average of two (2) cycle
lengths or 240 seconds of delay (whichever is less).

The two intersections that do not meet county operating standards are discussed below.

NE 124th Avenue/NE 119th Street
