available. Preliminary traffic signal warrants indicate that signalization is warranted based on four hour
and eight-hour volumes. We note that the in-process trips are adding a total of 334 AM peak hour trips
(a 46 percent increase over the existing total entering vehicles) and 451 PM peak hour trips (a 53 percent
increase over the existing total entering vehicles). Appendix “F” contains the signal warrants.

Year 2029 Total Traffic Conditions
The year 2029 total traffic conditions analysis forecasts how the study area’s transportation system will
operate with the traffic generated by the proposed development.


Proposed Development Plan
GHK Enterprises, Inc., proposes to develop up to 146 single-family homes on the study site. The proposed
site will provide vehicular and pedestrian connections between the existing Plateau Manor, approved
Heartwood Subdivision, and existing Fieldstone Estates developments. As previously shown in Figure 2,
vehicular access to the site is proposed via the eastern terminus of NE 109th Street, northern terminus of
NE 142nd Avenue and the western terminus of NE 111th Street. Driveway access to individual residential
homes will then be provided via the roadway network serving the property.


Trip Generation
Trips for the proposed subdivision were estimated using trip rates obtained from Trip Generation
Manual, 12th Edition (Reference 8), as shown in Table 7. The daily trips were estimated using the average
trip rate while the weekday AM and PM peak hour trip rates were estimated using fitted equations.

Traffic Operations
The year 2029 background traffic volumes for the weekday AM and PM peak hours (shown in Figures 6
and 7) were added to the site-generated traffic (shown in Figures 8 and 9) to arrive at the year 2029 total
traffic volumes. The weekday AM and PM peak-hour turning-movement volumes shown in Figures 10
and 11, respectively, were used to conduct an operational analysis at the study intersections to
determine the year 2029 total traffic operations.

Consistent with background traffic conditions, all but two study intersections are projected to operate
per the County’s adopted standards as specified in CCC Section 40.350.020.G. The same two intersections
that do not meet county operating standards under background conditions are forecast to continue to
experience long delays as discussed below. The NE 117 th Avenue/NE 119th Street intersection is projected
to operate at an overall LOS F during the PM peak hour; however, all individual movements satisfy the
County’s delay performance standard of an average of two (2) cycle lengths or 240 seconds of delay
(whichever is less). Appendix “G” contains the year 2029 total traffic conditions worksheets.

NE 124th Avenue/NE 119th Street
Consistent with background conditions, stop-controlled side street delay on the northbound approach is
projected to continue to result in LOS E conditions during the weekday AM and PM peak hours (LOS E
with a V/C ratio under 1.0) and the projected traffic volumes satisfy preliminary traffic signal warrants.
Major street turning and through movements are projected to operate at LOS B or better during both
peak hour analysis periods. The proposed site development is not expected to add any weekday AM or
PM peak hour trips to the stop-controlled northbound approach. Accordingly, no mitigation is
recommended in conjunction with the proposed site development per CCC Section 40.350.020.G.1.c.1
(the proposed development adds fewer than five (5) peak hour trips to the failing intersection approach).

NE 132nd Avenue/NE 119th Street
Consistent with background conditions, stop-controlled side street delay on the northbound approach is
projected to result in LOS F conditions during the weekday AM and PM peak hours (LOS F with a V/C ratio
above 1.0 under weekday AM conditions and below 1.0 under weekday PM conditions).

We recommend the proposed development widen the northbound NE 132 nd Avenue approach within
the existing public right-of-way to provide a northbound left-turn lane with at least 150 feet of storage
and a shared through/right-turn lane to mitigate the site-generated trip impacts. Table 8 below
summarizes the mitigated performance results restore the northbound intersection approach to better
than pre-development background conditions. Appendix “H” contains the 2029 mitigated total traffic
conditions worksheets for the NE 132nd Avenue/NE 119th Street intersection.

As shown in Table 9, three of the study concurrency corridor segments are projected to exceed the 0.90
V/C ratio criteria under year 2029 PM peak hour total traffic conditions.

The eastbound segment of NE 119th Street between NE 117th Avenue and NE 124th Avenue is projected
to operate at a V/C ratio of 1.10 (compared to 1.09 under background traffic conditions). The proposed
development is estimated to add 16 PM peak hour trips to this segment. We note NE 119th Street has
separate eastbound through and right-turn lanes at NE 122nd Avenue (local) and NE 124th Avenue
(regionally significant collector), increasing the theoretical eastbound carrying capacity at those two
public street intersections. The projected eastbound V/C ratio is less than 0.90 east of NE 124 th Avenue.
A more detailed operational analysis should be performed before the County makes any major design,
reconstruction or investment decisions for this corridor or future development fronting the roadway
segment.

Consistent with background conditions, the NE 99 th Street segment between NE 117th Avenue and NE
124th Avenue is projected to continue to operate at a V/C ratio over 0.90 with a forecast V/C ratio of 0.99
and 0.97 for the eastbound and westbound directions, respectively. The proposed development is
estimated to add 35 eastbound weekday PM peak hour trips and 21 westbound weekday PM peak hour
trips to this segment. The segment does not exceed a V/C of 1.00, meaning there is still capacity on the
roadway. The intersections of NE 124th Avenue/NE 99th Street and NE 117th Avenue/NE 99th Street are
expected to operate at an acceptable LOS and delay. Therefore, the over-capacity V/C ratio does not
represent a roadway deficiency, rather corridor mobility facilitated with acceptable signalized
intersection LOS. The NE 99th Street corridor segment appears to be constructed to its planned ultimate
3-lane configuration and it is unclear what, if any, additional capacity can be provided along the corridor.
A more detailed operational analysis should be performed before the County makes any major design,
reconstruction or investment decisions for this corridor.


SITE ACCESS CONSIDERATIONS
This section covers various site access considerations for the Heartwood North development.


NE 132nd Avenue & NE 114th Street Intersection Traffic Control Considerations
The Clark County Arterial Atlas (Reference 5) identifies a planned north/south minor arterial (M-2cb)
connection from the current southern terminus of NE 132nd Avenue south to NE 99th Street at NE 137th
Avenue. When this connection is constructed by others in the future, it is anticipated that the eastbound
and westbound approaches to the NE 132nd Avenue & NE 114th Street intersection will be stop-controlled,
and NE 132nd Avenue will operate as a free-flow major street movement. Future widening and
reconfiguration of the existing intersection approaches by others is anticipated as half-street
improvements are completed and the intersection evolves to its planned ultimate configuration.




Kittelson & Associates, Inc.                                                                   Portland, Oregon
Heartwood North TIA                                                                                 Project #: 31137
February 2026                                                                                               Page: 31


Sight Distance Review
Sight distance was not analyzed as the site access will be an extension of existing NE 109 th Street and NE
111th Street. On-site and off-site landscaping and any above ground utilities at the individual residential
driveways and along internal roadways should be installed and maintained to provide adequate sight
distance per Clark County requirements.


FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
The results of this transportation impact study indicate that the proposed Heartwood North development
can be developed while complying with Clark County concurrency requirements. The findings of this
analysis and our recommendations are discussed below.


Findings
                All study intersections operate acceptably during the weekday AM and weekday PM peak
                 hours under existing conditions.
                Historical crash data for the study area intersections indicate no patterns or trends that
                 require mitigation associated with the proposed Heartwood North development.
                All but two study intersections are projected to operate acceptably during the 2029
                 weekday AM and PM peak hours background traffic conditions:
                       o The NE 124th Avenue/NE 119th Street intersection is projected to operate at LOS E
                         under both AM and PM peak hour periods, and signal warrants are met.
                       o The NE 132nd Avenue/NE 119th Street intersection is projected to operate at LOS F
                         under both AM and PM peak hour periods, and Signal Warrant 1 (Eight-Hour) is not
                         met while Signal Warrant 2 (Four-Hour) is met.
                All but three study corridor segments operate within the County’s 0.90 V/C standard under
                 year 2029 background traffic conditions. The three segments that exceed this standard are:
                       o The eastbound segment of NE 119th Street between NE 117th Avenue and NE 124th
                         Avenue with a projected V/C ratio of 1.09.
                       o Both eastbound and westbound directions on NE 99 th Street between NE 117th
                         Avenue and NE 124th Avenue with projected V/C ratios at 0.94 and 0.95,
                         respectively.
                All but two study intersections are projected to operate acceptably during the 2029
                 weekday AM and PM peak hours total traffic conditions with the addition of site-generated
                 trips.
                       o The northbound NE 124th Avenue/NE 119th Street intersection approach is projected
                         to operate at LOS E under both AM and PM peak hour periods, and signal warrants

Kittelson & Associates, Inc.                                                                       Portland, Oregon
Heartwood North TIA                                                                                  Project #: 31137
February 2026                                                                                                Page: 32


                               are met. The proposed development is only projected to add vehicle trips to the
                               eastbound and westbound through movements and not to the northbound
                               approach that is operating at LOS E. Accordingly, no mitigation is recommended in
                               conjunction with the proposed site development per CCC Section 40.350.020.G.1.c.1
                               (the proposed development adds fewer than five (5) peak hour trips to the failing
                               intersection approach).
                       o The northbound approach to the NE 132nd Avenue/NE 119th Street intersection is
                         projected to operate at LOS F under both AM and PM peak hour periods. The site-
                         generated trip impact can be mitigated in conjunction with the proposed
                         development by widening the northbound NE 132 nd Avenue approach within the
                         existing public right-of-way to provide a northbound left-turn lane with at least 150
                         feet of storage and a shared through/right-turn lane.
                The same three concurrency corridor segments that exceed the County’s 0.90 V/C standard
                 under year 2029 background traffic conditions also do so under total traffic conditions as
                 follows.
                       o The eastbound segment of NE 119th Street between NE 117th Avenue and NE 124th
                         Avenue is projected to operate at a V/C ratio of 1.10.
                       o The segment NE 99th Street between NE 117th Avenue and NE 124th Avenue is
                         projected to operate at a V/C ratio of 0.99 and 0.97 for the eastbound and
                         westbound directions, respectively.


Recommendations
Based on the traffic operations analysis findings, we recommend the following in conjunction with the
proposed site development.
                The project widens the northbound NE 132nd Avenue approach within the existing public
                 right-of-way to provide a northbound left-turn lane with at least 150 feet of storage and a
                 shared through/right-turn lane.
                Above-ground utilities, monuments, fencing, and vegetation be appropriately located and
                 maintained on-site to preserve adequate intersection sight lines per Clark County Standards.

We trust this transportation impact study adequately addresses the traffic impacts associated with the
proposed Heartwood North development. Please contact us if you have any questions or comments
regarding the contents of this report or the analyses performed.

Comments
We live on a 20 acre parcel of what used to be categorized as AG-20 south of Dollars Corner with
a house and heritage barn built in 1917. The land is a part of the largest contiguous wetland of
Clark County out of the Ridgefield Wildlife Refuge and is part of the historic Patterson Swale. The
Clark County Public Utility planted and maintained a wetlands rehabilitation project along Mill
Creek on about 9 acres of our land. This project has increased habitat, helped with water purity,
and flood control along the creek. It has improved the tree canopy and carbon footprint of the
area. Since moving here 24 years ago, we have watched the continued degradation and paving
over of agricultural and green space and have seen 72nd avenue, 179th street, and 199th streets,
become congested and overused as apartments and homes have been built on what was once
agricultural land. We have experience increase flooding over 209th street caused by wetland
destruction in the process of home building. Moreover, we are very tired of hearing about building
"affordable" housing to deal with the un-housed county population, when builders get tax breaks
for "affordable" homes that start at $350,000 or a very few studio apartments in a large complex
that require a monthly rent of $1800. We urge you to develop policies designed to build up rather
than out and stick with the current urban growth boundaries. We urge the Council to limit urban
growth boundary expansion, to protect agricultural lands, and to ambitiously address greenhouse
gas emissions reduction targets, aligned with the city of Vancouver's Climate Action Framework
and in line with the Clark County Public Health Climate Action Program.

Southwestern Washington/Clark County because of its deeply rooted history in agriculture and
small land holdings and the quality of life that this produces for residents including obtaining
fresh produce directly from local farms. The county final EIS underlines that all forecasted
population and employment growth in Clark County can be accommodated within current UGAs.
The WA Dept of Commerce concurred with this and recently stated, “In our review of the draft
comprehensive plan and agricultural lands study, we did not find any discussion clearly
demonstrating that the lands proposed for de-designation no longer meet the designation
criteria.” The hundreds of acres that Ridgefield, La Center, and Camas are requesting to pave over
forever are designated prime agricultural lands and farmlands of statewide importance.
Additionally, Battle Ground’s proposed expansion would pave over hundreds of acres of rural
lands identified in the Agricultural Lands Study. These lands are a vital and needed resource with
respect to local food security, climate change resiliency, and agricultural jobs. The County should
honor the recommendations of the Agricultural Advisory Commission, which voted to maintain all
existing agricultural designations and requested a moratorium on upzoning of lands that meet the
legal criteria for agricultural designation. I urge the Council to adopt an alternative with no urban
growth area expansions.

The Transportation Element and Capital Facilities Plan Are Not Internally
Consistent
Submitted for inclusion in the index of record
Clark County Comprehensive Growth Management Plan — 2025–2045 Periodic Update
Re: Transportation Element (Chapter 5) and Transportation Capital Facilities Plan (Appendix A)
— planned transportation improvements do not support the allocated growth
To: Clark County Council and Community Planning
From: Heidi Pozzo
Date: September 30, 2026



The Council is preparing to adopt the 2025–2045 Comprehensive Plan Update, which allocates
32,960 housing units and 15,940 jobs to the unincorporated Vancouver urban growth area (Chapter
5, p. 8, lines 14–16). The Growth Management Act requires the transportation element and capital
facilities plan to identify the improvements that growth needs, show how they will be paid for, and
rest on assumptions compatible with the rest of the plan (RCW 36.70A.070; WAC 365-196-
500(2)). As drafted, they do not. The deficiency list, the modeled network, the Arterial Atlas, the
concurrency standard, and the funding plan each rest on different assumptions, and the plan does
not reconcile them.
In September, WSDOT reviewed the draft transportation capital facilities plan, and County staff
answered its comments. That exchange, read with the Planning Commission drafts of Chapter 5
and Appendix A, shows four ways the transportation system the plan relies on is not planned or
paid for:
  • The County and WSDOT are not working from the same list of problems. WSDOT did not
    know about locations the County flagged, and the County’s list leaves out locations
    WSDOT, the public, and the Final EIS have identified.
  • Growth the plan places on state corridors depends on state improvements that are
    unfunded, undefined, or in no state plan, and the state’s adopted Highway System Plan
    funds expansion last.
  • The County Road Fund, the local backstop, is projected to spend more on operations than it
    takes in from about 2038, shrinking what it can contribute to capital projects.
  • The plan measures need one way and approves development another. A ratio above 0.90 is
    a deficiency on a state route, while concurrency review approves development on County
    corridors above the same ratio.
The Salmon Creek Interchange Phase 2 project shows the first three. The County identified the
area’s road problems in 1997 and closed it to development with moratoria between 2001 and 2006.
Phase 2 was to finish the interchange fix that began with Phase 1. The County now states its scope
must be redefined and its feasibility study is unfunded, and the Regional Transportation Plan does


                                                1
not schedule even the study until 2036–2045. The plan still counts $35 million for it, and the 2045
analysis assumes the related interchange improvements are built.
These comments supplement my July 19, 2026 memorandum on internal inconsistency and
concurrency, my July 21, 2026 comments on the Transportation and Capital Facilities elements,
my August 16, 2026 memorandum on the Arterial Atlas, my August 19, 2026 comments on the
RTC travel demand model, and my September 23, 2026 submission, Clark County Does Not Have
an Operating Transportation Concurrency System, and do not repeat them.

Salmon Creek Interchange Phase 2 has been in the plans for years without a defined scope,
and the plan treats it as built and funded

Four points follow from Table 1.
   • The County project exists to complement WSDOT capacity improvements. For Phase 2,
     the record shows no WSDOT capacity project, only an unfunded study of whether one is
     feasible (WSDOT 6 and 23; response 6).
   • Phase 2 has been carried for years under shifting descriptions: “NE 134th St to I-205” in
     the 2014–2033 CFP (Appendix A, Table A.3), “improved access from NE 134th St to I-
     205” at $35 million in the 2024 RTP (Appendix N, p. 40), corridor improvements to
     complement WSDOT’s capacity improvements at the same $35 million in Table 9, and a
     scope that “would need to be updated or redefined” in the County’s response (response 6).
     Between the July 1 draft and the Planning Commission draft it moved into the funding
     analysis with no change in its definition.
   • Table 9 marks three projects as included in the funding analysis: Phase 2 at $35 million,
     NE 88th Street at $1.2 million, and NE Ward Road at $1.4 million, together $37.6 million.
     Table 15 carries $20.1 million for all Regional and Partnership Projects (Appendix A, pp.
     31 and 38). The $35 million for Phase 2 alone exceeds that entire category.
   • The 2045 analysis assumes the Salmon Creek interchange improvements are complete.
     Congestion that twice stopped development in this area is treated as solved in the model
     and funded in the financial plan, while both agencies state in writing that no project has
     been defined.
Appendix A also lists a Salmon Creek Corridor Planning Study for NE Salmon Creek Ave/NE
134th St from about NE 20th Ave to NE 50th Ave, to be done separately or with a Phase 2 planning
study (Appendix A, Table 12, p. 14).
Developer-commissioned traffic studies have shown the corridors around the interchange above
the 0.90 standard. A May 11, 2026 memorandum by the applicant’s traffic engineer in the 174th
Street Subdivision proceeding compiles 27 developer-commissioned studies prepared from 2018
through 2026 (PLD-2026-00002, Ex. 100). It reports NE 134th Street from NE 20th Avenue to NE
Salmon Creek Avenue at 1.03 to 1.12 in both peak hours; NE Salmon Creek Avenue from NE
134th Street to NE 50th Avenue at 1.08 in the AM peak; NE 139th Street from NE 20th Avenue
to NE 23rd Avenue at 0.917 to 1.24; and NE 10th Avenue from NE 139th Street to NE 149th Street
at 1.078 (Ex. 100, Table 1, p. 3).
The County has known about this area’s road problems since at least 1997, when most of the
Salmon Creek sub-area was placed in urban holding pending a road plan; County staff later found



                                                       3
most of that plan’s improvements impractical and cost-prohibitive (Salmon Creek Sub-Area Plan
TAC notes, March 10, 2010, p. 1). Between 2001 and 2006 the County imposed an interim urban
holding and two moratoria when the network at NE 134th Street fell behind development
(Appendix A, Table 26). When it extended the moratorium in 2005, the County found that the
remedy was high-cost interchange improvements for I-5 and I-205, which individual developers
could not provide (Ordinance 2005-07-21). The Salmon Creek Interchange was the response, in
two phases. Phase 1 was built. Phase 2 was to finish the job.
The problems Phase 2 was meant to address remain. WSDOT identifies intersection spacing on
NE 134th Street, the connection to the I-205 southbound on-ramp, and severe lane imbalance at
the NE 20th Avenue signal, and asks whether Phase 2 addresses them (WSDOT 6). The RTP
describes Phase II as improved access from NE 134th Street to I-205, at $35 million, with WSDOT
and Clark County as joint lead (Appendix N, p. 40). Appendix A’s $35 million matches that entry.
In conversation with County staff, I was told that Phase 2 is the remainder of the original Salmon
Creek Interchange Project, split off because there was not enough funding in 2013–2014 to
complete it; that the remaining work is primarily WSDOT’s optimization of the ramps on NE
134th Street, with the County’s corridor language in Table 9 added to flag other improvements it
would like considered with that investment; and that a study is needed to redefine the scope and
update the cost, since the $35 million was carried over from the RTP.
WSDOT pays for state work and the County for its own. The plan does not say whether the $35
million is the County’s share, WSDOT’s, or both, yet it counts the full amount in the County’s
funding analysis, and neither agency has a defined project to fund.
The only step with a defined path is a study, and it has no date. The County states the scope must
be redefined and the joint feasibility study is unfunded, with timing to be determined (response 6).
The RTP schedules that study for the same 2036–2045 window as the project, and RTC states that
most projects on its 20-year list have no identified funding source (Appendix N, pp. 7 and 40). A
project not studied until the last decade of the planning period cannot realistically be scoped,
designed, funded and built before 2045. Phase 2 is also not among the 17 regional projects, totaling
$740 million, for which the Clark County Transportation Alliance, whose supporters include Clark
County and RTC, asked the Legislature for directed funding in 2026. The RTP lists WSDOT and
the County as joint leads, consistent with each paying for its own part. Neither part is defined or
funded. A problem the County identified in 1997 will go unresolved until after 2045.
At the same time, the plan directs density to the areas that depend on this interchange, including
the NE 179th Street corridor, NE 50th Avenue and NE Salmon Creek Avenue, 11th Avenue and
164th Street, and NE 119th Street and NE 50th Avenue, all of which rely on the Salmon Creek
commercial area for daily needs. My July 19, 2026 memorandum (section 5) sets out how that
concentrates demand on the roads serving the commercial area.

The plan loads growth onto state corridors with limited or unfunded infrastructure
In response to WSDOT comment 22, the County agrees to add the 2024 Highway System Plan
funding order to Chapter 5:
   • First, fund operations, maintenance, capital preservation, and required programs such as
     fish passage.
   • Then, from what remains, spend $2 on safety and efficiency for every $1 spent on highway
     expansion.

will operate at an acceptable volume-to-capacity ratio “assuming completion of the RTP project

preservation and after safety and efficiency at two to one. The plan nonetheless allocates growth
that depends on these facilities functioning in 2045.
Appendix A says as much. It states that additional analysis and interagency coordination are
needed to define the County’s role, responsibility, and level of commitment for each regional
partnership project, and that a project left out of the funding analysis may reflect no expected
financial commitment from the County (p. 13, lines 13–16).
The Preferred Alternative zoning map places higher-density zoning at the edge of the urban
holding along NE 72nd Avenue and SR 503 (Preferred Alternative zoning map, June 25, 2026).
Those two roads are the north-south connections between the Vancouver urban growth area and
Battle Ground; C-TRAN’s Battle Ground route runs on SR 503 (Heartwood North TIA, p. 9). They
must carry both the housing the plan places along them and the traffic from the growth the plan
allocates to Battle Ground. SR 503 carries no cost or County improvement in Tables 9 and 10, and
the RTP’s only entry at SR 503/NE 119th Street is a study scheduled for 2036–2045. NE 72nd
Avenue carries two different costs in Appendix A, $83.5 million in Table 4 and $104,875,000 in
Table 19. The plan adds growth on both routes, and at the end of both, without a funded capacity
improvement on either.
WSDOT pays for state projects, and the County is not expected to fund them. The problem is
where the plan puts growth. It directs housing onto and beyond SR 503, SR 500, SR 502, I-5 at
179th Street, and the Salmon Creek interchange, where the state improvements those corridors
need are unfunded, undefined, or in no state plan. Tables 9 and 10 list state needs with no cost
(Appendix A, pp. 31–32), and WSDOT states none appears in any WSDOT plan or study (WSDOT
19, 20, 24). The RTP’s only entry at SR 503/NE 119th Street is a study scheduled for 2036–2045,
Salmon Creek Phase 2 has no defined scope, and the state’s funding order places expansion last.
For SR 500 from NE Fourth Plain Boulevard to NE 76th Street, which Table 9 lists with no cost
estimate (Appendix A, p. 31), WSDOT estimates $17 million to $19 million, and that cost is not
in the financial analysis (WSDOT comment 1). Where probable funding falls short of identified
needs, “including state transportation facilities,” RCW 36.70A.070(6)(a)(iv)(C) requires the
County either to show how the funding will be raised or to reassess its land use assumptions. For
these corridors the plan does neither. It keeps the growth where the state infrastructure is not
coming.

The County cannot fund its own projects
The $554 million shortfall is the gap in the County’s own financial plan: County roads, paid with
County Road Fund dollars, impact fees, REET, and the grants the County expects to win. RCW
36.70A.070(6)(a)(iv)(C) requires that, if probable funding falls short of identified needs, including
state transportation facilities, the plan discuss how additional funding will be raised or how land
use assumptions will be reassessed. County staff presented that requirement to the Council on July
15, 2026, alongside Figure 1.




                                                 8
My July 21, 2026 comments (paragraphs 3 through 7) set out the Road Fund projection, the
different dollar bases for costs and revenues, the funding options, and the grant-match problem.
This comment adds what the Planning Commission draft and the County’s responses show.
The cost side is not settled. Staff have updated Appendix A’s figures as the drafts progressed: the
July draft showed a shortfall of about $584.5 million on $1,605.8 million of expenditure, and the
Planning Commission draft shows $554 million on $1,496.2 million (Appendix A, p. 34; Table
15, p. 38). At the July 15, 2026 work session, staff stated that the transportation cost figures had
not been updated in several years and were expected to increase with inflation. Phase 2 is one
example: its $35 million is the figure carried over from the 2024 RTP, and staff have said an
updated estimate is needed. The $554 million shortfall is a floor, not an estimate.

 vehicle fee or 0.1% sales tax

Source: Appendix A pp. 48–49, Tables 23, 24 and 25.

At these amounts, every option combined yields at most about $230 million over twenty years,
less than half of the $554 million shortfall (Appendix A, p. 34). The local option gas tax accounts
for more than half of that and requires voter approval; the options the Council can adopt on its own
yield about $89 million.
Appendix A also carries different costs for the same project in different tables. NE 72nd Avenue
from NE 139th Street to NE 219th Street is $83.5 million in Table 4 and $104,875,000 in the
impact fee list (Table 19). NE Ward Road to SR 500 is $1.4 million in Table 9 and $1,125,000 in
Table 18 (Appendix A, pp. 19, 31 and 43).

The plan relies on a concurrency test the County is not applying
The County states the state route segments in Table 9 were flagged because they exceeded 0.9 v/c
(response 13). In the plan, a ratio above 0.90 is a deficiency on its own. Chapter 5 adopts the
County segment standard as a ratio that “shall not exceed 0.90” (p. 37, lines 1–4), and states that


                                                        10
the standards are used to identify deficient facilities for both capital planning and concurrency
management (p. 34, lines 2–3).
In concurrency review, it is not tested. As long as intersections operate within acceptable level of
service, staff treat a corridor ratio above 0.90 as one that “does not represent roadway deficiencies”
(Ex. 100, p. 2); my September 23, 2026 submission sets out that practice. The plan’s growth
allocation assumes a concurrency check that is not being applied.
CCC 40.350.020(G)(1)(a) requires V/C to be measured on state highways of regional significance.
County code does not set their capacity, and it should not, since state route standards are
WSDOT’s. In practice, developer studies supply the number. SR 503 is a state route, but it
functions more like an arterial. Ex. 100 nonetheless assigned it 2,000 vehicles per hour per
direction, the capacity the code gives the Pa-4b classification, the same figure used for Padden
Parkway (Table 1). That is a generous assumption for a signalized, congested arterial, and SR 503
still measures 0.928 to 1.066 with it. The County’s responses do not say what capacity its own
consultant used (response 13), nor do they explain the threshold. For state routes that are not
Highways of Statewide Significance, Chapter 5 adopts LOS E or better in urban areas (p. 42, lines
21–23), and its Table 5.04 equates LOS E with a ratio between 0.90 and 1.0.
The County also states that roads proposed in the Arterial Atlas were not included in the future
network used for the 2045 model run (responses 4 and 5). The plan’s deficiency analysis and the
Arterial Atlas rest on different road networks. The responses do not identify which network was
assumed for NE 179th Street.
My August 16 memorandum sets out the rest. The plan requires new bicycle facilities on 106.4
miles of County road outside the capital project list, deletes the policy clause that protected vehicle
lane capacity, and adopts an Arterial Atlas with no cross-section for a protected bike lane, buffered
bike lane, or shared-use path. Chapter 5 states the Atlas will be updated after adoption (p. 24, lines
12–15). Neither the Atlas classifications that set capacity in concurrency review nor the network
the RTC model was run on reflects any travel lane given up for those facilities. The road problems
this plan identifies are measured on roads with more travel lanes than the plan intends to leave in
place.

What the record establishes
  1. The County identified the Salmon Creek area’s road problems in 1997, and congestion
     produced development moratoria from 2001 through 2006. In 2005 the County found that
     the remedy was high-cost interchange improvements for I-5 and I-205.
  2. The County now states the Phase 2 scope must be redefined and its feasibility study is
     unfunded. WSDOT confirms the study is unfunded. The RTP schedules the study for 2036–
     2045, and Phase 2 is not among the projects the region asked the Legislature to fund in 2026.
     The Planning Commission draft moved Phase 2 into the funding analysis at $35 million, and
     the 2045 analysis assumes the interchange improvements are built.




                                                  11
 3. WSDOT states it was not aware of deficiencies the County flagged on SR 500, SR 502, and
    SR 503, and that no project in Tables 9 and 10 appears in any WSDOT plan or study.
 4. Three locations WSDOT identifies from its corridor plan, public complaints, and prior
    conversations with County staff are not in Tables 9 and 10 as drafted. Chapter 5 lists the I-5
    northbound deficiency between 179th Street and SR 502 among the state routes needing
    upgrades (Table 5.11); Appendix A Table 9 does not.
 5. The plan places growth on state corridors whose improvements are unfunded, undefined, or
    in no state plan, including SR 500, which WSDOT estimates at $17 million to $19 million,
    while the Highway System Plan funding order the County agrees to add places highway
    expansion last.
 6. The County’s own financial plan leaves a $554 million shortfall, which its funding options
    cover less than half of, with more than half of that dependent on voter approval. The County’s
    July 15 presentation shows the Road Fund’s net operating revenue available for capital
    falling below zero from about 2038, and staff have said the cost figures are out of date, so
    the shortfall is a floor.
 7. Developer-commissioned studies project the SR 503/NE 119th Street westbound approach
    WSDOT identified at LOS F by 2029, and show corridors around the Salmon Creek
    Interchange and on NE 179th Street above 0.90. None of the 27 studies compiled in Ex. 100
    reviewed I-5.
 8. The plan flags state routes as deficient above 0.90 volume-to-capacity, while concurrency
    review approves development on County corridors above 0.90 when intersections pass. The
    modeled network, the Arterial Atlas, and the multimodal level of service standards do not
    rest on the same assumptions.
 9. The plan directs density to the Salmon Creek/Fairgrounds area, which depends on the Salmon
    Creek interchange, and to NE 72nd Avenue and SR 503, without a funded capacity
    improvement on the routes that serve it.
Taken together, the transportation element and capital facilities plan are not internally consistent,
and they do not support the level of growth the Comprehensive Plan allocates. The deficiency list,
the modeled network, the Arterial Atlas, the concurrency standard, and the funding plan each rest
on different assumptions, and the plan does not reconcile them.

Appendix N: Plans, Studies, and Projects
The RTP is a living document and will continue to evolve and be updated on a regular basis to address a
number of long-term regional transportation projects, programs, plans, and studies that require further
monitoring, evaluation, and policy decisions prior to inclusion in the RTP. The 20-Year RTP Projects
included in this appendix are composed of regional and local planned projects. This appendix
summarizes the range of transportation studies, plans, programs, and projects that, combined, achieve
the RTP’s vision and that are also identified to help get closer to implementing the RTP’s transportation
goals: Economic Vitality and Quality of Life, Safety and Security, Accessibility and Mobility, and
Sustainability and Resiliency (refer to Chapter 3). RTC will continue to engage and collaborate with
regional partners and stakeholders to ensure the successful implementation of this plan as we
collaborate with our planning partners in the development of studies, plans, and programs and
implement projects in the RTP lists and action strategies proposed in this plan.



Projects, Programs, Plans, and Studies

Interstate Bridge Replacement Program (IBR)
The Interstate Bridge is a critical connection between Oregon and Washington, located on Interstate 5
where it crosses the Columbia River. Replacing the aging Interstate Bridge across the Columbia River
with a modern, earthquake resilient, multimodal structure that provides improved mobility for people,
goods, and services is a high priority for Oregon and Washington. The IBR program is a renewed effort
jointly led by the Oregon Department of Transportation and the Washington State Department of
Transportation, in collaboration with eight regional partner agencies: Oregon Metro, Southwest
Washington Regional Transportation Council, TriMet, C-TRAN, City of Portland, City of Vancouver, Port
of Portland, and Port of Vancouver. These partners serve on an Executive Steering Group that provides
regional leadership recommendations to the program. The IBR program continues to work with the
program partner agencies, stakeholders, and public to identify the best possible multimodal solution.


I-5 and I-205 Regional Mobility Pricing Project (RMPP)
The Regional Mobility Pricing Project (RMPP) will apply congestion pricing on all lanes of Interstate-5
and Interstate-205 to manage travel demand and traffic congestion on these facilities in the Portland,
Oregon metropolitan area in a manner that will generate revenue for transportation system
investments. The pricing varies by time of day according to a set schedule, which can be updated


                                                                            Regional Transportation Plan, 2024
Appendix N: Plans, Studies, and Projects                                                                    2



periodically by the Oregon Transportation Commission. Higher fees will be charged during peak travel
periods (such as morning and evening peak hours) and lower fees during off-peak hours. Congestion
pricing is intended to encourage motorists to plan travel in advance and allows traffic to flow more
freely during peak times.

The process to implement a toll program requires substantial analysis, public input, construction,
testing, and education before the system can be operational. The earliest tolling could begin under the
Regional Mobility Pricing Project is 2026.


Cascadia High-Speed Rail Study
The Cascadia High-Speed Rail Study proposes to connect people and communities, increase economic
competitiveness, and improve quality of life across the Cascadia megaregion. This fast, safe, predictable
way to travel would connect the metro areas of Vancouver, B.C.; Seattle, WA; Portland, OR, and points
between and beyond. With equity as a guiding principle, the high-speed rail project could help connect
local workers to family-wage jobs, increase access to affordable housing choices, and offer greater
mobility for almost 9 million people. This project is also part of a growing movement to mitigate the
impacts of climate change by using clean energy. Rather than relying on congested highways or
increasing air traffic, the high-speed rail project offers a sustainable alternative to traveling greater
distances quickly and reliably. Study recommendations will be evaluated as appropriate for inclusion
into the Regional Transportation Plan.

In fall 2021 the states of Washington and Oregon and the province of British Columbia signed a
Memorandum of Understanding to continue to advance this work. In December 2023 Cascadia High-
Speed Rail and Amtrak Cascades were accepted into USDOT’s Corridor Identification and Development
Program, bringing formal federal funding and participation. WSDOT, ODOT, and the B.C. Ministry of
Transportation and Infrastructure continue to collaborate with partners along the corridor to shape
future planning and development activities.


Columbia Connects
Columbia Connects is a regional project intended to strengthen the bistate partnership between Oregon
and Washington. Centered around the ecosystem of industries and work sheds that are interconnected
by the Columbia River, the project seeks to develop a clear understanding of the conditions within this
subdistrict; the shared economic and community values of the region; and the strategies, projects, and
programs needed to achieve desired outcomes. Columbia Connects provides a shared investment
strategy that outlines specific opportunities for investment based on feasibility, effectiveness, equity,
and input from project champions. Convened by Metro and RTC, the partners will finalize and carry out
actions included in a shared investment strategy, continuing to partner across state boundaries to
establish agreements and commitments for implementation and ongoing coordination on resource
acquisition.




                                                                            Regional Transportation Plan, 2024
Appendix N: Plans, Studies, and Projects                                                                     3



Clark County Freight Mobility Study
The 2009 Clark County Freight Mobility Study was developed to provide an understanding of the key
elements of freight movement and to explain why freight and goods movement is important to Clark
County’s economy and employment. The study inventoried existing freight and goods movement and
identified current deficiencies and future action items to be addressed as part of ongoing regional and
local planning processes. In addition, the study began to identify corridor investment needs to sustain
jobs and economic development for existing and future industrial and employment centers. The Clark
County Freight Mobility Study will be updated in 2024.

Washington State Freight Plan
As the secondmost trade-dependent state per capita in the USA, Washington relies heavily on an
efficient freight transportation network. The freight system supports 1.41 million jobs in freight-
dependent industries in Washington, with a gross business income of $550.5 billion. Freight and goods
are shipped into, out of, and around Washington by truck, rail, air, pipeline, and water.

The Washington State Freight System Plan was completed and certified by the Federal Highway
Administration on December 1, 2017. The freight plan addresses multimodal freight transportation and
speaks of three components of the freight transportation system:

  •     Global Gateways, which provides freight access to international markets;
  •     Made in Washington, providing transportation for freight that is manufactured or produced in
        Washington; and
  •     Delivering Goods to You, representing local freight delivery for businesses and residents.


Washington State Rail Plan
In Washington State, freight rail needs are addressed in Washington State Department of
Transportation’s (WSDOT’s) 2019 Washington State Rail Plan. The plan serves as a blueprint for public
investment in the state’s rail transportation system.


Truck Parking Action Plan
The Truck Parking Action Plan recommends various options and strategies to address the shortage of
truck parking in Washington State and provides a summary of truck parking issues and potential
solutions to identify the gap in need vs. availability of truck parking in Washington State, as well as
possible options to address the issue. In addition, it includes an action plan for Washington State, with
specific next steps for the highest priority actions. The solutions identified will address immediate needs
and set the State up for long-term success in addressing the issue.


METRO’s Regional Freight Strategy Study
This study seeks to identify and produce increases in rail capacity, safety, land use compatibility, and
operational efficiencies to support freight and goods movement in the region, which is important to our



                                                                             Regional Transportation Plan, 2024
Appendix N: Plans, Studies, and Projects                                                                    4



long-term economic and environmental sustainability and will help to maintain the region’s competitive
advantage in a global marketplace. This strategy will provide a coordinated vision and approach for
enhancing freight and goods movement and prioritizing freight investments based on clear priorities.


Washington Transportation Plan
The Washington Transportation Plan (WTP) is the state’s long-range transportation plan, based on the
Legislature’s six policy goals: economic vitality, preservation, safety, mobility, environmental & health,
and stewardship. This 20-year vision for improving the state’s transportation network is completed in
two parts: policy and implementation. The policy plan, 2040 & Beyond, provides statewide policy
recommendations to the Legislature. The implementation plan, Washington Transportation Plan,
Phase 2 - Implementation 2017-2040, applies key policy recommendations for the WTP to further
develop the state’s complex transportation system through four focus areas: maintain and preserve
assets; manage growth and traffic congestion; enhance multimodal connections and choices; and align
the funding structure with the multimodal vision. The Washington Transportation Plan is being updated.
It is anticipated that the plan update will be completed by the end of 2025.


Clark County Comprehensive Economic Development Plan
The Columbia River Economic Development Council (CREDC) adopted its Clark County Comprehensive
Economic Development Plan in August 2017. The plan includes goals to expand the existing base
industry clusters in the region, including computer and electronic, clean tech, software, metals and
machinery, and life sciences. Goal 2 includes support for the region’s people by developing a resilient
economy. Goal 3 relates to creating places, including making employment areas shovel ready and
determining regional transportation needs to support economic development.


Clark County Employment Land Study
In 2016 CREDC adopted the Clark County Employment Land Study. This study is an economic
development and policy tool for civic leaders and policymakers. The study identified 56 employment
sites that are 20 acres and larger throughout Clark County. The study considers the market, land use,
and physical characteristics to assess site readiness. The RTP includes projects that will support
economic development and access to employment lands.


Clark County’s Comprehensive Growth Management Plan
Clark County’s Comprehensive Growth Management Plan (Plan) is a long-range policy guide for how the
County plans to manage growth and development over a 20-year period. The Plan is required by the
Growth Management Act. The plan contains elements comprised of existing conditions, goals, policies,
and strategies to accomplish the Plan’s goals. Consideration of transportation system improvements
responsive to the growth management plans will be a priority to optimize public and private
investments in regional and local transportation infrastructure.



                                                                            Regional Transportation Plan, 2024
Appendix N: Plans, Studies, and Projects                                                                       5



Transportation Corridor Visioning Study
The RTC Board endorsed the Transportation Corridor Visioning Study in April 2008. The Visioning Study
recommendations presented broad concepts for new regional corridors, corridors connecting places,
and current and potential future nodes of growth in Clark County. Corridors on the eastside (north-
south) connections between east Vancouver/Camas/Washougal and Battle Ground, east-to-west
connections between Battle Ground and the Discovery Corridor, and westside connections were all
considered. The Visioning Study recommendations concluded that further regional land use planning
review and analysis is needed prior to further review of potential new corridors in order to gauge
whether future growth forecasts warrant such a project discussion. The study also recommended that
future study should include review of the impacts of these candidate corridors on future land use
patterns within Clark County. That analysis should occur during a future countywide Growth
Management Planning comprehensive plan process.


Human Services Transportation Plan (HSTP)
RTC’s Human Services Transportation Plan addresses the transportation needs of those with mobility
challenges and special transportation needs, including people with disabilities, the elderly, the young,
low-income populations, and rural residents unable to provide their own transportation. The first HSTP
for this region—which includes Clark, Skamania, and Klickitat counties—was adopted in 2007. Plan
updates followed in 2011, 2014, 2018, and 2022. A plan update is required at least every four years. The
intent of the Human Services Transportation Plan is to identify transportation needs and solutions and
thereby improve transportation services for people with disabilities; seniors; and, in general, those
unable to drive themselves. Development of a Human Service Transportation Plan ensures that
communities coordinate transportation resources provided through multiple federal programs. A
coordinated plan can help to enhance transportation access, minimize duplication of services, and
encourage the most cost-effective transportation possible.


Washington Statewide Human Services Transportation Plan
The Statewide Human Services Transportation Plan serves as a strategic framework for addressing the
state’s existing and future human services transportation needs. The plan was developed through
collaboration with affected stakeholders and with public input. The Statewide HSTP provides a set of
goals and strategies to facilitate coordination and maximize resources to meet the transportation needs
of the most vulnerable people in our state.


C-TRAN Transit Development Plan
C-TRAN’s Transit Development Plan is a long-range, comprehensive strategy for enhancing public
transportation for Clark County residents over the next 20 years. C-TRAN’s plan is designed to respond
to growing transportation needs and the need to provide expanded, reliable, and safe service.
Maintaining and expanding transit service is vital for ensuring the economic vitality and quality of life of
the region.



                                                                              Regional Transportation Plan, 2024
Appendix N: Plans, Studies, and Projects                                                                    6



Clark County High Capacity Transit (HCT) Study
The Clark County High Capacity Transit System Study was adopted in December 2008 following a two-
year planning process. The HCT plan provided a blueprint for C-TRAN and the Clark County region to
move high capacity transit improvements forward in identified HCT corridors. The HCT System Study
assumes that traffic volumes will increase over time as planned growth and economic development
continue in the Clark County region. The constrained ability to expand highway capacity in several key
regional transportation corridors is expected to worsen traffic, increasing the need to develop a
transportation alternative.

Projects and strategies resulting from these studies will be addressed further as part of the
Comprehensive Growth Management planning process and future RTP updates. If projects are identified
and considered feasible, further detailed analysis and financial modeling may be warranted prior to
inclusion into the fiscally constrained RTP.


Washington State Active Transportation Plan
The Active Transportation Plan - 2020 and Beyond is a compass for creating the future of walking, biking,
and rolling on or across state highways in Washington. It is used in decisions to help connect people to
where they want to go, whether they use active transportation for the whole trip or just a part of it,
such as walking to a bus stop, riding a bike to work, or rolling home from a ferry terminal.


Regional Active Transportation Plan for Clark County
The Active Transportation Plan addresses objectives, policies, goals, the regional active transportation
system network, programs, and projects. It describes the status of walking, bicycling, and rolling and
access to transit in the Clark County region. The plan provides a needs assessment that considers user
demand for active transportation, equity, and safety considerations. These analyses can help decision-
makers understand where to target resources to have the greatest impact on improving active
transportation in Clark County. This plan can be found on Appendix F.


Clark County Bicycle and Pedestrian Master Plan
In November 2010 the Board of Clark County Commissioners approved the Clark County Bicycle and
Pedestrian Master Plan to make it safer and more convenient for people to get to major destinations in
our region on foot or by bicycle. The plan identifies ways to improve the transportation network by
integrating existing sidewalks, bike lanes, and trails. The plan points out that this will require design
standards that work well with Clark County’s transportation network for motor vehicles.




                                                                            Regional Transportation Plan, 2024
Appendix N: Plans, Studies, and Projects                                                                      7



Clark County Parks and Open Space Plan
The Parks, Recreation, and Open Space (PROS) Plan is a six-year plan that anticipates the programming
and capital projects necessary to meet the community’s needs for parks, recreation, and open space, as
well as trails. This plan identifies local, regional, and national growth trends in recreational activities
such as walking, cycling, team sports, and picnicking. The PROS Plan for Clark County is a functional part
of the County’s Comprehensive Plan. It provides a six-year strategic plan and policy framework to meet
the county’s park and recreational needs. The purpose of the plan is twofold: to meet Growth
Management Act (GMA) requirements and to set forth a six-year capital facilities program for park
development and acquisitions focused on gaps in levels of service; asset diversity; and diversity, equity
and inclusion.


Regional Emergency Transportation Route Update
The designated Regional Emergency Transportation Routes (RETR) for the five-county Portland-
Vancouver metropolitan region—which includes Clackamas, Columbia, Multnomah, and Washington
counties in Oregon and Clark County in Washington—was updated in 2021. Although this effort is
primarily focused on updating the RETR for emergency response immediately following a large seismic
event, considerations for other natural hazards—such as flooding, wildfire, and severe weather—will be
incorporated into the data set and project recommendations for future consideration, including work to
support transportation recovery planning. A second phase of follow-up work will be proposed to
prioritize/tier the updated routes and develop operational guidance for route owners/operators.


20-Year RTP Projects
The 20-Year RTP project list includes planned projects that are on the regional transportation system, as
well as local arterial projects that are not on the designated system. The majority of these projects do
not have an identified funding source but are still community priorities for implementation during the
RTP’s 2045 planning horizon.

� URGENT NEIGHBORHOOD ALERT: Massive
Zoning Changes in Pleasant Valley-October 1st
Did you know our neighborhood is about to be rezoned for massive high-density
apartments and multi-family complexes?
The Clark County Council is on the verge of adopting a new 20-year Comprehensive
Growth Management Plan. If approved, it will force much of our semi-rural Pleasant
Valley area into high-density zones. Single-family homes will be restricted to tiny 4,000-
square-foot lots, while large apartment complexes and attached multi-family dwellings
will become dominant.

How This Impacts Our Immediate Area (NE 50th Ave & 139th St):
   •   Severe Traffic Bottlenecks: NE 139th Street and NE 50th Avenue are already
       highly congested. Forcing hundreds of new high-density units into this pocket will
       cause gridlock trying to access I-205 and local thoroughfares.
   •   Parking Chaos: The county's plan cuts multi-family parking minimums down to
       just 0.5 spaces per unit. This means overflow vehicle parking will completely
       pack our narrow residential streets.
   •   Overcrowded Schools: Pleasant Valley Elementary and Middle schools sit right in
       this immediate zone. Our classrooms and school infrastructure are simply not
       equipped to handle a sudden housing surge.

           Unpleasant Valley Neighborhood

How High-Density Upzoning with Massive Apartment Blocks will
Destroy Your Way of Life------Don’t Let it Happen!!!

Developing a property under low-density zoning compared to
high-density multifamily zoning fundamentally changes the built
environment and community dynamics. In jurisdictions like Clark
County, R1-7.5 is a low-density single-family residential zone
(typically requiring 7,500 square feet per lot), whereas R32 and
R36 are high-density multi-family zones allowing up to 32 and 36
dwelling units per acre, respectively.

Here is how the exact same piece of land would compare under
these three designations:

� Visuals and Physical Appearance
 • R1-7.5 Development: This yields a traditional suburban
   landscape. The property would be subdivided into detached,
   single-family homes (usually 1 to 2 stories) with individual
   driveways, private front/back yards, and street-facing
   garages. Greenspace is fragmented across private lawns.

  •   R32 & R36 Developments: These are apartment complexes,
      condominiums, or dense townhome blocks. In Eastern
      Europe they are referred to as “Commie Blocks” reminiscent
      of the Soviet Occupation era. Buildings are typically 3 to 4+
      stories high to maximize air rights. Instead of individual
      yards, you will see consolidated communal greenspaces,
      courtyards, large asphalt parking lots, or parking structures.
      In a sense they are “Commie Blocks”, as they are forced on
      us by state and local governments who take away our
      individual freedoms, personal security, wealth and well-being
      in an attempt to provide it to others. It is destined to fail as it
      always has because quality of life is something you have to
      work for.


  •   R32 vs. R36: Visually, these two are highly similar. However,
      an R36 zone allows a slightly higher footprint or minor height
      increases (e.g., tighter building separations or an extra
      fraction of a story) to squeeze in those 4 additional units per
      acre.

� Traffic Impact on Neighbors
 • R1-7.5 Development: Traffic generation is low and highly
   predictable. Peak flows occur tightly during school drops
   and work commutes. Vehicles are mostly contained within
   private garages and driveways, minimizing persistent on-
   street overflow.

  •   R32 & R36 Developments: Traffic volume increases
      exponentially. A one-acre lot transitions from roughly 4
      single-family homes to 32 or 36 households. This introduces
      multi-directional traffic at all hours of the day (including
      delivery drivers, ride-shares, and visitors).

  •   The Parking Factor: Depending on local updates to the Clark
      County development code, multi-family developments often
      have reduced parking space minimums per unit (sometimes
      lowered significantly to incentivize affordability). This
      frequently results in an overflow of cars parked on adjacent
      neighborhood streets, reducing street walkability and
      visibility.
� Crime and Public Safety
 • The "Density vs. Crime" Reality: Criminological data shows
   that higher density does not inherently cause crime.
   However, high-density residential properties can change the
   nature of local policing and neighborhood security.

  •   R1-7.5 Development: Relies heavily on traditional "territorial
      reinforcement"—meaning neighbors easily spot strangers,
      and clear property lines make trespassing obvious (the "eyes
      on the street" effect).

  •   R32 & R36 Developments: Multifamily developments feature
      high anonymity, making it harder for residents to distinguish
      between a neighbor and a stranger in common spaces. This
      anonymity results in a higher volume of property crimes (like
      package theft and car break-ins), robust security features
      such as perimeter fencing, keycard gates, and 24/7 security
      cameras are often a necessity.

� Noise and Activity Levels
 • R1-7.5 Development: Ambient noise levels are generally low.
   Noise is sporadic and domestic—lawnmowers, kids playing,
   or occasional backyard gatherings.

  •   R32 & R36 Developments: Ambient noise is continuous and
      mechanical. You will experience frequent noise from
      communal HVAC systems, garbage trucks emptying
      dumpster enclosures, car alarms, and doors slamming in
      parking lots. Internally and externally, living walls are closer
      together, meaning a higher baseline of conversational and
      foot-traffic noise. The higher ambient noise floor is simply
      due to the tight clustering of mechanical infrastructure
      required to support a massive number of people in a small
      space.
